tamil:
மனைவிழைவார் மாண்பயன் எய்தார் வினைவிழைவார்
வேண்டாப் பொருளும் அது.
transliteration:
Manaivizhaivaar maanpayan eydhaar vinaivizhaivaar
ventaap porulum adhu.
current_meaning: Those who give themselves over to doting on their wives miss life's highest fruit; and that very indulgence is what people intent on real accomplishment choose to avoid.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a team captain who stops practising because he only wants to hang out at home all day. He may be comfortable, but the team never wins. People who want to do big things keep their comfort in balance with their work.
university_explanation: The chapter title penvazhich seral (பெண்வழிச் சேறல்) literally means 'going by a woman's way', and Parimelazhagar frames the whole chapter as advice to a ruler or man of affairs within the Porul (polity) section, placed among other vices to be avoided (chapters 92-94 on wanton women, drink and gambling). In this opening couplet manai-vizhaivaar (மனைவிழைவார், those who crave the wife or household pleasure) fail to reach maan-payan (மாண்பயன், the excellent fruit), which Parimelazhagar glosses as aram (virtue), while vinai-vizhaivaar (வினைவிழைவார், those who desire action) reject such indulgence as a hindrance to porul (wealth-making). Textual note: ytamizh and thirukkural.net read the third word as vinaivizhaiyaar (வினைவிழையார், 'those who do not desire action'), while thirukkural.com, kuraltheni.com and Parimelazhagar's own gloss read vinaivizhaivaar; we follow the latter. Also note that thirukkural.com wrongly prints Kalaignar's gloss for Kural 801 under this verse. Modern critics point out that the chapter assumes a male, elite reader and a patriarchal household; many contemporary readers (including Mu. Varadarasanar's 'considering domestic comfort paramount') take its target to be infatuation and neglect of duty rather than women as such, a reading supported by Valluvar's high praise of the wife in chapter 6 (வாழ்க்கைத் துணைநலம்).

tamil:
பேணாது பெண்விழைவான் ஆக்கம் பெரியதோர்
நாணாக நாணுத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Penaadhu penvizhaivaan aakkam periyadhor
naanaaka naanuth tharum.
current_meaning: The prosperity of a man who neglects his own responsibilities and gives himself wholly to desire for his wife becomes a great public embarrassment and brings shame upon himself.
elementary_explanation: If a class president stops doing the job and just lets his best friend decide everything, the whole class feels let down, and he ends up embarrassed too. Holding a job means doing it yourself.
university_explanation: Penaadhu (பேணாது, 'without guarding/caring for') is read by Parimelazhagar as neglecting one's own aanmai (ஆண்மை, manliness, i.e. capacity for independent action), while pen-vizhaivaan (பெண்விழைவான்) is one who desires the 'femininity' of his wife. The aakkam (ஆக்கம், prosperity) he holds becomes a periyadhor naan (பெரியதோர் நாண், a great shame) first for men generally and then for himself; Parimelazhagar explains that because the wife effectively controls the giving and enjoyment of that wealth, the public sees the man's agency as transferred to her. Manakkudavar reads penaadhu as neglecting aram and porul (virtue and wealth). Kalaignar's modern gloss shifts the emphasis to a man who abandons his principles to chase a woman, illustrating the trend among twentieth-century commentators to recast the chapter as a critique of infatuation rather than of women's agency. The text is uniform across ytamizh, thirukkural.net, thirukkural.com and kuraltheni. Contemporary critics note that the verse's notion of 'shame to all men' reflects a gendered honour code of its era.

tamil:
இல்லாள்கண் தாழ்ந்த இயல்பின்மை எஞ்ஞான்றும்
நல்லாருள் நாணுத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Illaalkan thaazhndha iyalpinmai egngnaandrum
nallaarul naanuth tharum.
current_meaning: The unnatural habit of cowering before one's wife will always make a man feel ashamed in the company of good people.
elementary_explanation: If you are always too scared to say what you think, even to someone you love, you may feel awkward around friends who speak up honestly. Love works best when both people can speak freely.
university_explanation: Iyalpinmai (இயல்பின்மை) means 'that which is not natural', and Parimelazhagar glosses the whole phrase as the fear (achcham) that makes a man stoop (thaazh) before his wife; within his patriarchal frame, it is 'unnatural' because he expects the wife to be the deferential one. He adds that when a husband is so cowed, no one guides the household and every fault follows, so he is ashamed among the nallaar (நல்லார், the good) at all times (எஞ்ஞான்றும்). Manakkudavar reads it simply as the ruinous habit of stooping to the wife. Kalaignar narrows it to a husband who fails to correct a wife lacking good character, and Solomon Pappaiah stresses fear, showing modern commentators softening the verse toward a critique of timidity. The text is identical in all four sources consulted. Modern readers rightly note that the assumption that deference is natural only for wives is a historical norm, not a universal truth, while the verse's underlying point about a fear-driven partnership remains discussable.

tamil:
மனையாளை அஞ்சும் மறுமையி லாளன்
வினையாண்மை வீறெய்த லின்று.
transliteration:
Manaiyaalai anjum marumaiyi laalan
vinaiyaanmai veereydha lindru.
current_meaning: A man who lives in fear of his wife, and so forfeits the merit that leads to a good hereafter, will never win acclaim for his work, however capable he may be.
elementary_explanation: A painter who is too afraid of anyone's opinion to paint what he really sees will never make a great painting. Fear holds back good work.
university_explanation: Marumai-ilaalan (மறுமையிலாளன்) means 'one without (merit for) the next world'; Parimelazhagar explains that such a man cannot perform the duties of the householder (illaram) properly and so loses the reward of the hereafter. Vinai-aanmai (வினையாண்மை, the capacity to direct undertakings) may exist, but it will not attain veeru (வீறு, distinction, acclaim) among the good, because one who lacks his own nature cannot bring work to completion. Manakkudavar adds that this verse means such a man will not create wealth. Textual note: ytamizh, thirukkural.net and thirukkural.com divide the line as 'வீறெய்த லின்று' while kuraltheni prints 'வீறெய்தல் இன்று'; this is a difference of word-spacing (சீர் division vs. word division), not wording. Kalaignar gives a distinctive modern reading, taking the man as one who fears to undertake married life at all, a reinterpretation that avoids the gendered fear. Contemporary critics observe that the verse links domestic authority to public efficacy in a way typical of premodern political ethics.

tamil:
இல்லாளை அஞ்சுவான் அஞ்சுமற் றெஞ்ஞான்றும்
நல்லார்க்கு நல்ல செயல்.
transliteration:
Illaalai anjuvaan anjumat regngnaandrum
nallaarkku nalla seyal.
current_meaning: A man who is afraid of his wife will always be afraid even to do good things for good people.
elementary_explanation: If you are scared to share your snack with a hungry classmate because someone might be cross with you, fear is stopping you from being kind. Kindness needs a little courage.
university_explanation: Parimelazhagar glosses nallaar (நல்லார், the good) as gods, ascetics, the wise, one's two elders (parents) and worthy guests, and nalla seyal (நல்ல செயல்) as giving them what they need; even when the wealth is his own earning, the fearful husband hesitates. He supports the reading with a parallel from the Jain Tamil epic Civaka Cintamani (மண்மகள் 217): 'illaalai anji virunthin mugam kondra nenjin pullaalan', a man who, fearing his wife, turned away the face of a guest. Manakkudavar sums the verse as meaning such a man cannot practise aram (virtue). Kalaignar inverts the sense, reading that a man anxious not to err in doing good will heed a watchful wife, a strikingly egalitarian modern reinterpretation. The text is identical across the four sources. Critics note that the verse presumes hospitality and charity are the husband's prerogative, a presumption that modern readers can retain as a call to generosity without its gendered frame.

tamil:
இமையாரின் வாழினும் பாடிலரே இல்லாள்
அமையார்தோள் அஞ்சு பவர்.
transliteration:
Imaiyaarin vaazhinum paatilare illaal
amaiyaardhol anju pavar.
current_meaning: Even if they live as splendidly as the gods, men who are afraid of their wife's slender, bamboo-like arms have no real dignity.
elementary_explanation: A superhero with amazing powers is not much of a hero if he is too scared to act. What makes someone admirable is courage, not just strength or riches.
university_explanation: Imaiyaar (இமையார், 'the unblinking ones') is a classical Tamil epithet for the gods; paatu (பாடு) here means dignity or worth, and paatilar those lacking it. Amai-aar-thol (அமையார்தோள்) compares the wife's shoulders or arms to amai (bamboo), a conventional image of feminine grace; Parimelazhagar notes that the slender image heightens the irony: a warrior who conquered heroes' arms yet fears these gentle ones has no aanmai (manliness). He reads 'living like the gods' as the life of heroes who reached heaven through valour, and says this verse closes a group of four (903-906) on the fault of fearing the wife. Manakkudavar takes it to mean that even the wealthy are not respected by others. Kalaignar again reinterprets, aiming the criticism at men who submit to a wife merely for beauty, not for wisdom or character. The text is uniform across sources. Modern critics note the verse's equation of dignity with masculine dominance as a historically situated value.

tamil:
பெண்ணேவல் செய்தொழுகும் ஆண்மையின் நாணுடைப்
பெண்ணே பெருமை உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Penneval seydhozhukum aanmaiyin naanutaip
penne perumai utaiththu.
current_meaning: The modest dignity of a woman is worthier than the so-called manhood of a man who lives only by running his wife's errands.
elementary_explanation: Being a grown-up does not mean being bossy, and it does not mean just following orders either. A person with self-respect, whoever they are, deserves more admiration than someone who has given up thinking for themselves.
university_explanation: Pen-eval (பெண்ணேவல்) is 'a woman's command', and the man who 'conducts himself doing it' (seydhu ozhugum) is contrasted with naanutaip penne (நாணுடைப் பெண்ணே), the woman possessed of naan (நாண், modesty, sense of shame). Parimelazhagar notes that 'modest woman' is added deliberately as the opposite of the shameless man: the wife who issues commands is not the point of comparison, but rather womanhood marked by naan, which he regards as superior to such manhood. He also observes the emphatic separation of 'penne' at the line's start. Manakkudavar reads that such men are not respected by others. The verse is notable because, within its gendered frame, it affirms that a woman's perumai (பெருமை, greatness) can exceed a man's; modern feminist readers note, however, that it values women for modesty while denying men the role of following a woman. Text is identical across sources.

tamil:
நட்டார் குறைமுடியார் நன்றாற்றார் நன்னுதலாள்
பெட்டாங்கு ஒழுகு பவர்.
transliteration:
Nattaar kuraimutiyaar nandraatraar nannudhalaal
pettaangu ozhuku pavar.
current_meaning: Those who live only as their fair-browed wife wishes will neither meet the needs of their friends nor do any good deed.
elementary_explanation: If you only ever do what one person wants, you might forget to help your other friends when they need you. Good friends keep room in their life for everyone who counts on them.
university_explanation: Nattaar (நட்டார்) are those who have formed friendship (natpu), and kurai mudiyaar (குறைமுடியார்) means they will not fulfil their friends' needs; nandru aatraar (நன்றாற்றார்) means they will not perform good deeds, which Parimelazhagar specifies as aram that aids the next world. Nan-nudhalaal (நன்னுதலாள், 'she of the fair forehead') is a conventional epithet he compares with 'bamboo-like shoulders' in 906, and pettaangu (பெட்டாங்கு) means 'as she desires'. His reasoning is that the wife cannot herself command and give wealth for these purposes, so both this-worldly and other-worldly duties lapse. Fitting the chapter's place in the Natpiyal (friendship) section, the verse highlights obligations to friends. The text is uniform across sources; Sivayogi Sivakumar's playful gloss reading pettaangu as 'like a pottu (forehead mark)' is a modern pun, not the classical sense. Modern readers may take the general point that any single relationship which crowds out duties to friends and community is unhealthy.

tamil:
அறவினையும் ஆன்ற பொருளும் பிறவினையும்
பெண்ஏவல் செய்வார்கண் இல்.
transliteration:
Aravinaiyum aandra porulum piravinaiyum
peneval seyvaarkan il.
current_meaning: Virtuous deeds, well-earned wealth and even other pleasures are all absent from those who simply do whatever their wives command.
elementary_explanation: A good life has three parts: being kind, working hard, and having fun. If someone lets another person run every part of their life, they can end up missing all three.
university_explanation: This verse maps directly onto the three aims of the Kural itself: aram (அறம், virtue), porul (பொருள், wealth) and, as Parimelazhagar glosses pira-vinai (பிறவினை, 'other deeds'), inbam (இன்பம், pleasure). He explains that once virtue and wealth are gone, even pleasure is lost because its direction lies with the wife, and he notes that verses 907-909 together treat the fault of doing the wife's bidding (eval). Manakkudavar adds that even men without fear, if they simply obey, lose all three. Textual note: some editions print pen-eval as one word (பெண்ணேவல்), as in 907, while all four sources consulted print 'பெண்ஏவல்' here. Kalaignar narrows the target to men enslaved by arrogant women's orders, a reading that limits the claim. Contemporary scholars stress that Valluvar's ideal of the wife elsewhere (chapter 6) is a partner who safeguards the household, and that the chapter's real target is the abdication of one's own judgment.

tamil:
எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சத் திடனுடையார்க்கு எஞ்ஞான்றும்
பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை இல்.
transliteration:
Enserndha nenjath thitanutaiyaarkku egngnaandrum
penserndhaam pedhaimai il.
current_meaning: Those whose minds are given to careful thought and who have the strength and means that follow from it will never fall into the folly of being wholly ruled by attachment to a woman.
elementary_explanation: When you think things through and stay steady inside, you do not get swept away by any one wish or person. A calm, thoughtful mind keeps you in charge of your own choices.
university_explanation: En-serndha nenjam (எண்சேர்ந்த நெஞ்சம்) is 'a mind joined to deliberation'; Parimelazhagar takes it as a mind engaged in planning affairs of state, and reads idan (இடன்) not as 'firmness' (as some modern glosses do) but as 'wealth/means', citing Kural 218 ('இடனில் பருவத்தும்') and Kalittokai to establish that sense. Ytamizh's 'thitan' transliteration reflects the sandhi 'நெஞ்சத் திடன்', which modern commentators such as Kalaignar and Mu. Varadarasanar also read as thidan (திடன், firmness of mind), so both readings circulate. Pen-serndhaam pedhaimai (பெண்சேர்ந்தாம் பேதைமை) is the folly arising from attachment to the wife; Parimelazhagar says this folly is the root of all three faults treated earlier, namely desiring, fearing and obeying, so the closing verse sums up the chapter negatively. Manakkudavar explains en-serdhal as discerning the faults that arise from such attachment. Read today, the chapter's enduring core is this closing ideal of deliberative self-command, while its gendered framing belongs to its historical setting.

tamil:
அன்பின் விழையார் பொருள்விழையும் ஆய்தொடியார்
இன்சொல் இழுக்குத் தரும்.
transliteration:
Anbin vizhaiyaar porulvizhaiyum aaydhodiyaar
insol izhukkuth tharum.
current_meaning: The sweet words of bangle-adorned women who want a man not out of love but for his money will in the end bring him disgrace and grief.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a kid who suddenly calls you their best friend every day you bring a big bag of candy, and ignores you on days you bring nothing. Their nice words feel good, but they were never about you, and trusting them only ends with hurt feelings. Real friendship is liking someone, not liking what they can give you.
university_explanation: The opening couplet sets the chapter’s key contrast between anbu (அன்பு, love) and porul (பொருள், wealth): the women described here vizhaiyaar, ‘do not desire’, out of love but porul-vizhaiyum, ‘desire wealth’. Aaydhodiyaar (ஆய்தொடியார், ‘those wearing choice bangles’) is a conventional ornamental epithet, and the danger lies in their insol (இன்சொல், sweet speech), the same virtue Valluvar praises in chapter 10, here turned into a tool of profit. Izhukku (இழுக்கு) means both moral lapse and resulting disgrace; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah render it as ‘suffering’, Sivayogi Sivakumar as ‘degradation’. Parimelazhagar places the chapter in the Natpiyal (section on friendship) right after Penvazhicheral (being led by one’s wife), and reads it as a warning against an intimacy that only imitates friendship. The text is identical in ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பயன்தூக்கிப் பண்புரைக்கும் பண்பின் மகளிர்
நயன்தூக்கி நள்ளா விடல்.
transliteration:
Payandhookkip panburaikkum panbin magalir
nayandhookki nallaa vidal.
current_meaning: Weigh carefully the conduct of characterless women who first measure what they can gain from a man and then talk sweetly of virtue, and keep away from them.
elementary_explanation: Some people check how much pocket money you have before deciding how friendly to be, and then talk about how loyal they are. Valluvar says: notice that pattern, think about it, and do not get close to someone who measures you by your wallet.
university_explanation: The couplet rests on a play of the verb thookku (தூக்கு, ‘to weigh, to measure’): the women payan-thookki, ‘weigh the profit’, so the wise man must nayan-thookki, ‘weigh their character’, and then nallaa vidal (நள்ளா விடல்), ‘leave without joining’. There is also deliberate irony in panburaikkum panbin magalir, ‘women of no virtue (panbu) who speak of virtue’: the speech is a performance tuned to the size of the purse. Puliyur Kesigan reads nayan as their behaviour, while Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as the ‘pleasure’ they offer, which the wise man evaluates and declines. Parimelazhagar treats the couplet as a practical rule of discernment rather than a moral sermon, in keeping with the Porutpal’s concern with prudent conduct. No textual variants appear between ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பொருட்பெண்டிர் பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம் இருட்டறையில்
ஏதில் பிணந்தழீஇ அற்று.
transliteration:
Porutpendir poimmai muyakkam iruttaraiyil
edhil pinandhazheei atru.
current_meaning: The false embrace of women who want only money is like hugging a stranger’s corpse in a dark room: there is no warmth or feeling in it at all.
elementary_explanation: Think of hugging a big cardboard cut-out of a friend in the dark. It is shaped like a person, but nobody is really there to hug you back. Valluvar says that affection bought with money is like that: it looks like love, but there is no real heart inside it.
university_explanation: Kural 913 is the chapter’s most startling simile. Porut-pendir (பொருட்பெண்டிர், ‘women of wealth’, i.e. women who are for wealth) offer a poimmai muyakkam (பொய்ம்மை முயக்கம், false embrace), compared to clasping an edhil pinam (ஏதில் பிணம், a stranger’s corpse) in an iruttarai (இருட்டறை, dark room). Parimelazhagar’s gloss, followed by Puliyur Kesigan and by the bracketed ‘(hired men)’ in the standard English explanation, explains the image: it is the hired corpse-bearer who handles an unknown body in the dark for pay, without any bond, so the transaction is equally loveless on both sides. Kalaignar reads it as acting out love purely for money. The form thazheei (தழீஇ) is an alapedai (lengthened vowel) form of thazhuvi, ‘having embraced’. Both base sources agree on the text.

tamil:
பொருட்பொருளார் புன்னலந் தோயார் அருட்பொருள்
ஆயும் அறிவி னவர்.
transliteration:
Porutporulaar punnalan thoyaar arutporul
aayum arivi navar.
current_meaning: People of wisdom, who seek the true wealth of grace and compassion, will not touch the cheap charms of those for whom money is the only thing that matters.
elementary_explanation: If you are saving up for something really valuable, like a bicycle, you do not spend it all on sweets that are gone in a minute. Wise people treat their hearts the same way: they look for real kindness, not for ‘friendships’ that are only about money.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a pun on porul: porut-porulaar (பொருட்பொருளார்) are ‘those whose object (porul) is wealth (porul)’, set against arut-porul (அருட்பொருள்), ‘the wealth that is arul (grace, compassion)’, which the wise aayum (ஆயும், examine and pursue). Punnalam (புன்னலம், ‘petty or base beauty’) is the low pleasure they decline, and thoyaar (தோயார்) means ‘will not immerse themselves in or touch’. Mu. Varadarasanar treats arul itself as the highest wealth, while Solomon Pappaiah reads arut-porul as ‘wealth sought together with compassion’, a reading in keeping with Parimelazhagar’s concern that riches be earned and used with arul. The echo of chapter 25 (Aruludaimai) is deliberate. Ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net agree, with punnalan(th) sandhi spelled புன்னலந்.

tamil:
பொதுநலத்தார் புன்னலம் தோயார் மதிநலத்தின்
மாண்ட அறிவி னவர்.
transliteration:
Podhunalaththaar punnalam thoyaar madhinalaththin
maanda arivi navar.
current_meaning: Those whose understanding has been perfected by good natural sense will not seek the low pleasures of women whose favors are offered to anyone who pays.
elementary_explanation: A smart kid who knows what real friendship is will not chase someone who is ‘best friends’ with whoever gives the most presents that day. Good sense helps you see that kind of friendship is not really for you at all.
university_explanation: Podhu-nalaththaar (பொதுநலத்தார்) means ‘those whose charms (nalam) are common (podhu)’, available to all who pay. Valluvar sets this against mathi-nalam (மதிநலம்), ‘the excellence of natural intelligence’, which makes knowledge maandu (மாண்ட, perfected, excellent). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan distinguish iyarkai arivu (inborn sense) from acquired learning, and Kalaignar explicitly names both ‘natural intelligence and learned knowledge’, following Parimelazhagar’s distinction between mathi (native wit) and arivu (learning). The couplet is built parallel to 914 (punnalam thoyaar repeats), so the pair should be read together: 914 names the motive of the wise (arul), 915 the faculty (mathi). Both base sources give the same text.

tamil:
தந்நலம் பாரிப்பார் தோயார் தகைசெருக்கிப்
புன்னலம் பாரிப்பார் தோள்.
transliteration:
Thannalam paarippaar thoyaar thagaiserukkip
punnalam paarippaar thol.
current_meaning: Those who care about their own good name will not seek the arms of women who, proud of their charm, offer their cheap favors to all who pay.
elementary_explanation: If you care about being known as honest and kind, you will be careful about who you spend your time with. You would not team up with someone who sells their ‘friendship’ to anyone, because you value your good name.
university_explanation: The couplet repeats the verb paarippaar (பாரிப்பார்) in two senses: those who paarippaar thannalam, ‘cherish or spread their own goodness (or fame)’, will not touch the shoulders of those who paarippaar punnalam, ‘spread their petty charms abroad’. Thagai-serukki (தகைசெருக்கி) is ‘being proud of their attractiveness or skill’. Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesigan take thannalam as one’s own fame, Mu. Varadarasanar as one’s ‘good conduct’, and Parimelazhagar as the reputation that comes from virtue. Textual note: thirukkural.net prints the first verb as பாரப்பார் (paarappaar), whereas ytamizh.com and the standard Parimelazhagar text read பாரிப்பார்; the repeated verb and all four commentaries support பாரிப்பார், so the variant looks like a typographical slip.

tamil:
நிறைநெஞ்சம் இல்லவர் தோய்வார் பிறநெஞ்சிற்
பேணிப் புணர்பவர் தோள்.
transliteration:
Nirainenjam illavar thoyvaar piranenjir
penip punarpavar thol.
current_meaning: Only those who lack a steady, self-governed heart will seek the arms of women who embrace them while their own hearts are set on something else.
elementary_explanation: Someone who is pretending to be your friend while really thinking about your video games is not giving you their heart. Valluvar says only a person who cannot control their own wishes keeps running after friends like that.
university_explanation: Nirai-nenjam (நிறைநெஞ்சம்) is ‘a full or restrained heart’; nirai is the classical virtue of self-control, the power to hold the mind in check, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as ‘the strength to rule one’s heart’. The women are those who embrace while pira-nenjil peni (பிறநெஞ்சிற் பேணி), ‘cherishing something else in their heart’, which Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah identify as the money they want. The couplet thus contrasts two divided states: the women’s hearts are elsewhere, and the men lack a governed heart of their own. Parimelazhagar connects nirai with the self-mastery praised in chapter 13 (Adakkamudaimai). Both base sources agree on the text.

tamil:
ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்க்கு அணங்கென்ப
மாய மகளிர் முயக்கு.
transliteration:
Aayum arivinar allaarkku anangenba
maaya magalir muyakku.
current_meaning: For those who lack the wisdom to look closely, the embrace of deceitful women is said to be like being seized by an enchanting spirit that leads them to ruin.
elementary_explanation: In fairy tales, a magic song can make people forget who they are and walk into trouble. Valluvar says that people who do not stop to think can be ‘enchanted’ by false affection in the same way, while thoughtful people can see the trick.
university_explanation: Anangu (அணங்கு) in Sangam usage is a dangerous divine power, often a female spirit that seizes and afflicts; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as anangu-thaakku, ‘the attack of an anangu’, and as ‘Mohini’s bewitchment’, and Solomon Pappaiah as ‘a deity who stirs desire and takes life’. Maaya magalir (மாய மகளிர்) are women skilled in maayam (மாயம், deception, illusion). The decisive phrase is aayum arivinar allaar (ஆயும் அறிவினர் அல்லார்), ‘those who are not of examining intelligence’: only they experience this as a supernatural seizure, whereas the discerning see an ordinary deception. Enba (என்ப, ‘they say’) marks this as received opinion. Sivayogi Sivakumar alone reads anangu in the positive sense of ‘divine’, as what the foolish mistake such embraces for. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
வரைவிலா மாணிழையார் மென்தோள் புரையிலாப்
பூரியர்கள் ஆழும் அளறு.
transliteration:
Varaivilaa maanizhaiyaar mendhol puraiyilaap
pooriyargal aazhum alaru.
current_meaning: The soft arms of jewelled women who keep no limits are a hell-like mire into which base, undiscerning men sink.
elementary_explanation: Picture a pretty field that is really a deep mud bog. It looks soft and inviting, but anyone who walks in without thinking gets stuck and sinks. Valluvar says that ‘love’ that is only bought and sold is like that bog.
university_explanation: This couplet supplies the chapter’s title word: varaivilaa (வரைவிலா), ‘without varaivu’. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses varaivu as ‘a moral limit’ (ozhukka varaiyarai), and Puliyur Kesigan and Solomon Pappaiah as ‘not distinguishing between high and low’ among those who pay; in akam poetry varaivu also means ‘marriage’, which yields the reading ‘women outside wedlock’. Maanizhaiyaar (மாணிழையார்) is ‘those with fine jewels’. Alaru (அளறு) means both mire or mud and naraka (hell), and the commentators exploit both: Kalaignar speaks of ‘the mire called hell’. Puraiyilaa pooriyargal (புரையிலாப் பூரியர்கள்) are ‘base men without worth’; Sivayogi Sivakumar takes purai as ‘fault’, so ‘those who do not know what is wrong’. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
இருமனப் பெண்டிரும் கள்ளும் கவறும்
திருநீக்கப் பட்டார் தொடர்பு.
transliteration:
Irumanap pendirum kallum kavarum
thiruneekkap pattaar thodarbu.
current_meaning: Double-minded women, strong drink and gambling dice are the companions of those whom good fortune has abandoned.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a kid who spends all their allowance on silly gambling games at the fair, sugary junk, and ‘friends’ who only like them for their money. Soon the money is gone and so are the ‘friends’. Valluvar says these habits are a sign that someone’s good luck is slipping away.
university_explanation: The closing couplet groups three ruinous attachments: irumanap pendir (இருமனப் பெண்டிர், ‘women of two minds’, whose heart is in one place and body in another, as Solomon Pappaiah explains), kal (கள், toddy or liquor) and kavaru (கவறு, dice). Their thodarbu (தொடர்பு, ‘association’) belongs to those thiru-neekkap-pattaar (திருநீக்கப் பட்டார்), ‘those from whom Thiru has been removed’; Thiru is both fortune and the goddess Lakshmi (Thirumagal), which is how Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesigan read it. Parimelazhagar notes that the couplet links this chapter to the next two, Kallunnaamai (93, not drinking) and Soodhu (94, gambling), so it works as a hinge for the whole cluster of vices. Both sources agree on the text.

tamil:
உட்கப் படாஅர் ஒளியிழப்பர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகு வார்.
transliteration:
Utkap pataaar oliyizhappar enjnjaandrum
katkaadhal kondozhugu vaar.
current_meaning: Those who live with a constant craving for liquor are never held in awe by their enemies, and they lose the lustre of the good name they once had.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a strong, respected team captain who starts doing something silly every day. Soon nobody on the other team worries about him any more, and even his own friends stop looking up to him. The Kural says a love of strong drink does exactly that: it makes a person look small.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with two losses: the drinker is not utkappadaar (உட்கப்படாஅர், 'not feared', from உட்கு, awe or dread, with an alapedai lengthening) and he oliyizhappar (ஒளியிழப்பர், 'loses his lustre'), where oli (ஒளி) means both brightness and reputation. The habitual sense comes from katkaadhal kondozhuguvaar (கட்காதல் கொண்டொழுகுவார்), 'those who conduct themselves holding a love of toddy', so the target is addiction rather than a single lapse. Because the chapter sits in Porutpaal beside Varaivin Magalir (92) and Soothu (94), the traditional reading inherited from Parimelazhagar treats it as one of the vices a ruler must shun; Puliyur Kesikan's gloss on thirukkural.net explicitly makes the subject 'kings' whose enemies no longer fear them and who lose the fame won by their ancestors. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the subject general. The couplet is identical on ytamizh and thirukkural.net, though the two sites attach the Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar glosses in opposite order.

tamil:
உண்ணற்க கள்ளை உணில்உண்க சான்றோரான்
எண்ணப் படவேண்டா தார்.
transliteration:
Unnarka kallai unilunka saandroraan
ennap padavendaa thaar.
current_meaning: Do not drink liquor. If anyone must drink, let it be only those who do not care to be thought well of by good and wise people.
elementary_explanation: Suppose a teacher says, ‘Don't cheat on the test. Well, if you really want to cheat, go ahead, but only if you don't care whether anyone ever trusts you again.’ The teacher isn't giving permission. She is showing how much it costs. The Kural speaks about drinking the same way.
university_explanation: The first clause is a flat prohibition, unnarka kallai (உண்ணற்க கள்ளை, 'drink not toddy'). The second, unil unka (உணில் உண்க, 'if you would drink, drink'), is an ironic concession, a figure the commentators call igazhchchi (இகழ்ச்சி, scorn). It limits the 'permission' to those who are saandroraan ennappada vendaathaar (சான்றோரான் எண்ணப்பட வேண்டாதார்), people who do not wish to be esteemed by the saandror (சான்றோர், the noble and learned). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all keep this ironic reading. Puliyur Kesikan adds that the first clause is addressed to arivudaiyor (the wise), since toddy clouds the mind. The structure foreshadows Kural 923, where the saandror again sit in judgment. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
ஈன்றாள் முகத்தேயும் இன்னாதால் என்மற்றுச்
சான்றோர் முகத்துக் களி.
transliteration:
Eendraal mugaththeyum innaadhaal enmatruch
chaandror mugaththuk kali.
current_meaning: Drunkenness is painful to see even for the mother who bore a person, who forgives almost anything. How much worse must it look to the wise, who tolerate no fault?
elementary_explanation: Your mom loves you no matter what, even after you spill juice on the carpet. But some behaviour makes even a loving mom sad and embarrassed. If something upsets the person who forgives you most, imagine how it looks to a strict teacher or a respected elder.
university_explanation: The couplet argues from the lesser to the greater. Eendraal (ஈன்றாள், 'she who bore') is the most forgiving witness a person has; Puliyur Kesikan glosses her as the one who rejoices whatever her child does. Even 'in her face' (mugaththeyum, முகத்தேயும்) kali (களி, intoxication) is innaadhu (இன்னாது, painful). The question en matru (என் மற்று, 'what, then?') carries the argument to the saandror (சான்றோர்), whom Mu. Varadarasanar describes as having the nature of rebuking faults (குற்றம் கடியும் இயல்பு). The repeated mugam (முகம், face) presents shame as something seen. Kalaignar reads the subject as the son his mother cannot bear to look at. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
நாண்என்னும் நல்லாள் புறங்கொடுக்கும் கள்ளென்னும்
பேணாப் பெருங்குற்றத் தார்க்கு.
transliteration:
Naanennum nallaal purangodukkum kallennum
penaap perungutrath thaarkku.
current_meaning: The noble lady called Modesty turns her back and leaves those who commit the great and hateful fault called drink.
elementary_explanation: Picture Modesty as a kind lady who walks beside you and whispers ‘don't do that, it's embarrassing.’ The Kural says that when someone gets drunk she turns around and walks away, so there's no one left to stop him doing shameful things.
university_explanation: Naan (நாண், modesty, the sense of shame) is personified as a nallaal (நல்லாள், a good woman). Purangodukkum (புறங்கொடுக்கும்), literally 'gives the back', is a battlefield term for retreat, so Modesty flees from the drinker as a beaten warrior flees. The parallel compounds naanennum nallaal / kallennum penaap perungutram (கள்ளென்னும் பேணாப் பெருங்குற்றம், 'the great fault called toddy, which none would cherish') set a personified virtue against a personified vice. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses that she will not stand before the drinker; Solomon Pappaiah renders it as Modesty showing her back and going away. The idea looks ahead to Naanudaimai (chapter 102). The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
கையறி யாமை உடைத்தே பொருள்கொடுத்து
மெய்யறி யாமை கொளல்.
transliteration:
Kaiyari yaamai udaiththe porulkoduththu
meyyari yaamai kolal.
current_meaning: To pay good money in order to buy a state where you no longer know yourself shows a person who does not understand what he is doing.
elementary_explanation: Imagine spending all your pocket money on a ticket for a ride that makes you so dizzy you can't remember your own name, and then trips you over. You'd be paying to lose yourself. The Kural says buying liquor is that kind of bad deal.
university_explanation: The couplet balances two forms of ignorance: kaiyariyaamai (கையறியாமை) and meyyariyaamai (மெய்யறியாமை). The second clearly means not knowing one's own body or self, the stupor that porul koduththu (பொருள்கொடுத்து, 'by giving wealth') one kolal (கொளல், 'takes on'). The first is read in two ways. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as not knowing what to do, a failure of practical sense. Puliyur Kesikan (thirukkural.net) reads it as having one's past karma as its cause, so only an ill-fated person would make such a bargain. Kalaignar calls it folly beyond words. The Kural's irony is economic: wealth, the subject of Porutpaal, is spent to buy unawareness. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
துஞ்சினார் செத்தாரின் வேறல்லர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
நஞ்சுண்பார் கள்ளுண் பவர்.
transliteration:
Thunjinaar seththaarin verallar enjnjaandrum
nanjunpaar kallun pavar.
current_meaning: Just as sleepers are no different from the dead, those who drink liquor are always no different from people who swallow poison.
elementary_explanation: When someone is fast asleep, they can't see, hear or help anyone, almost as if they weren't there at all. The Kural says drinking liquor is like taking a little poison: it switches off your mind the same way.
university_explanation: The couplet is an udhaaranam (உதாரணம், exemplum) built on two equations. Thunjinaar (துஞ்சினார், those asleep) are 'not different from' (verallar, வேறல்லர்) seththaar (செத்தார், the dead), because both lack awareness. Likewise kallunbavar (கள்ளுண்பவர், toddy-drinkers) are always nanjunbaar (நஞ்சுண்பார், poison-eaters). Mu. Varadarasanar gives the shared term as arivu mayangudhal (அறிவு மயங்குதல், clouding of understanding). Puliyur Kesikan applies enjnjaandrum (எஞ்ஞான்றும், 'always') to the second clause: the drinker is permanently poisoned, while the sleeper only appears dead for a while. Kalaignar reverses the order and reads it as a hyperbole. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
உள்ளொற்றி உள்ளூர் நகப்படுவர் எஞ்ஞான்றும்
கள்ளொற்றிக் கண்சாய் பவர்.
transliteration:
Ullotri ulloor nagappaduvar enjnjaandrum
kallotrik kansaai pavar.
current_meaning: Those who drink in secret until their eyes droop will have their secret found out by their own townspeople, who will always laugh at them.
elementary_explanation: If you sneak cookies before dinner, the crumbs on your shirt give you away. The Kural says people who drink in secret are the same: their sleepy, drooping eyes tell everyone, and the whole neighbourhood ends up laughing.
university_explanation: The verb otri (ஒற்றி, 'in hiding') is used twice. Kal otri (கள்ளொற்றி) is drinking toddy secretly, and ul otri (உள்ளொற்றி) is the townsfolk spying out what is inside. Kansaaibavar (கண்சாய்பவர்) are 'those whose eyes droop', the physical sign that betrays them. Ulloor (உள்ளூர், one's own town) makes the mockery (nagappaduvar, நகப்படுவர், 'will be laughed at') come from neighbours, not strangers. Mu. Varadarasanar reads ul otri as the townsfolk probing into hidden matters. Kalaignar stresses that the reeling eyes cannot be hidden. thirukkural.net prints the couplet without the closing full stop; the wording is otherwise identical on both base sites.

tamil:
களித்தறியேன் என்பது கைவிடுக நெஞ்சத்து
ஒளித்ததூஉம் ஆங்கே மிகும்.
transliteration:
Kaliththariyen enbadhu kaividuka nenjaththu
oliththadhooum aange migum.
current_meaning: Let the drinker stop claiming ‘I have never been drunk’, because the moment he drinks, whatever he has hidden in his heart comes out even more.
elementary_explanation: It's like a shaken bottle of fizzy drink: open it and everything inside comes spraying out. The Kural says drink opens people up the same way, so pretending you never drink doesn't work. Your secrets fizz out the moment you do.
university_explanation: Kaliththariyen (களித்தறியேன்) is the drinker's own denial: 'I have never known intoxication.' Kaividuka (கைவிடுக, 'give it up') tells him to drop the lie. The reason is nenjaththu oliththadhooum (நெஞ்சத்து ஒளித்ததூஉம், 'even what was hidden in the heart'; the -ooum is an alapedai of -um, 'even') aange migum (ஆங்கே மிகும், 'there and then increases', that is, comes out all the more). Mu. Varadarasanar reads the hidden thing as the hidden fault; Puliyur Kesikan as the earlier concealment of drinking itself; Kalaignar as the truth that the drunk man blurts out. The idea is close to the Graeco-Roman proverb 'in wine, truth'. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
களித்தானைக் காரணம் காட்டுதல் கீழ்நீர்க்
குளித்தானைத் தீத்துரீஇ அற்று.
transliteration:
Kaliththaanaik kaaranam kaattudhal keezhneerk
kuliththaanaith theeththureei atru.
current_meaning: Trying to reason with a drunk man is like searching with a burning torch for someone who has sunk deep under water.
elementary_explanation: Imagine your friend has dived to the bottom of a pool and you try to find him by shining a candle from the side. The water puts the flame out and you can't reach him. The Kural says giving good reasons to someone who is drunk is like that: your words can't get through.
university_explanation: Kaaranam kaattudhal (காரணம் காட்டுதல், 'showing reasons') is set against keezhneer kuliththaan (கீழ்நீர்க் குளித்தான், 'one who has plunged into deep water'), and the attempt is theeththureei atru (தீத்துரீஇ அற்று, 'like searching with fire'). Thuru (துருவுதல்) means to probe or search, and the -eei is an alapedai lengthening. The image works twice over: fire cannot burn under water, and a drowned man is beyond help. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it as trying to sober or reform the drinker with arguments. Puliyur Kesikan takes kaaranam kaattudhal as pointing to another drunk as a warning, which leads into Kural 930. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
கள்ளுண்ணாப் போழ்திற் களித்தானைக் காணுங்கால்
உள்ளான்கொல் உண்டதன் சோர்வு.
transliteration:
Kallunnaap pozhdhir kaliththaanaik kaanungaal
ullaankol undadhan sorvu.
current_meaning: When a drinker is sober and sees someone else reeling drunk, does he not think that he looks the same when he drinks?
elementary_explanation: Have you ever laughed at someone acting silly, then realised you act just like that sometimes? The Kural asks why a drinker, seeing another person drunk and stumbling, doesn't think, ‘Oh no, that's me when I drink!’
university_explanation: The closing couplet is a rhetorical question marked by kol (கொல்). When the drinker, in kallunnaap pozhdhu (கள்ளுண்ணாப் போழ்து, 'the time he is not drinking'), sees a kaliththaan (களித்தான், a drunk man), will he not reflect, ullaan (உள்ளான், 'will he not consider'), on the sorvu (சோர்வு, slackness, lapse) that comes from his own drinking? The appeal is to self-recognition. Commentators agree on this reading: Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Puliyur Kesikan all take it as a sober drinker seeing his own condition in another. Mu. Varadarasanar's printed gloss reads மயங்கினவளை ('the intoxicated woman') on both base sites, apparently a typographical slip for மயங்கினவனை. The text is identical on ytamizh and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வேண்டற்க வென்றிடினும் சூதினை வென்றதூஉம்
தூண்டிற்பொன் மீன்விழுங்கி அற்று.
transliteration:
Vendarka vendridinum soodhinai vendradhooum
thoondirpon meenvizhungi atru.
current_meaning: Do not desire gambling even if you are able to win, because the winnings are like the bait a fish swallows along with the iron hook hidden inside it.
elementary_explanation: A fish sees a tasty worm and gulps it, happy for one second, but the worm hides a sharp hook. Valluvar says winning at gambling is that worm: it feels like a prize, but it pulls you in and you cannot get away.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by closing the most tempting loophole: vendridinum (வென்றிடினும், 'even should you win') concedes the gambler's best case and still forbids the desire (vendarka, வேண்டற்க). The simile turns on thoondirpon (தூண்டிற்பொன்), where pon (பொன்), usually 'gold', is read by the commentators as 'metal, iron': Mu. Varadarasanar on both ytamizh and thirukkural.net glosses it as தூண்டில் இரும்பு, 'the iron of the hook', and Kalaignar speaks of the iron barb (இரும்பு முள்). The alapedai in vendradhooum (வென்றதூஉம்) gives emphasis: even the thing won. The tradition descending from Parimelazhagar reads this chapter, like the two before it (Varaivin Magalir and Kallunnaamai), as a list of pleasures a ruler and a householder must shun, and the opening couplet sets the theme that gambling's gains are themselves the trap. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும் சூதர்க்கும் உண்டாங்கொல்
நன்றெய்தி வாழ்வதோர் ஆறு.
transliteration:
Ondreydhi noorizhakkum soodharkkum undaangol
nandreydhi vaazhvadhor aaru.
current_meaning: Gamblers gain one and lose a hundred; can there ever be, for such people, a way of living that reaches anything good?
elementary_explanation: Imagine trading a hundred of your marbles for the chance to win one. You would soon have none left. Valluvar asks: if someone keeps doing that, how could life ever go well for them?
university_explanation: The couplet works through a stark ratio, ondreydhi noorizhakkum (ஒன்றெய்தி நூறிழக்கும், 'gaining one, losing a hundred'), and then a rhetorical question ending in -kol (உண்டாங்கொல், 'will there be?'), which expects the answer no. Soodhar (சூதர்) means gamblers; aaru (ஆறு) is 'way, path', so nandreydhi vaazhvadhor aaru is 'a path of living that attains good'. The particle -um in soodharkkum ('even for gamblers') implies that other sinners may still find such a path, but gamblers, as a class, are shut out. Puliyur Kesikan on thirukkural.net softens the arithmetic to 'losing by hundreds out of the hope of gain', and Kalaignar reads it psychologically: a single win lures the player on into a hundred losses. Both base-text sites agree on the wording.

tamil:
உருளாயம் ஓவாது கூறின் பொருளாயம்
போஒய்ப் புறமே படும்.
transliteration:
Urulaayam oovaadhu koorin porulaayam
pooip purame padum.
current_meaning: If a person keeps endlessly calling out stakes on the rolling dice, his wealth and the income that sustains it will leave him and fall into the hands of others.
elementary_explanation: A king who spends all day shouting bets at a dice board has no time left to look after his kingdom. Little by little, his treasure and his lands end up in other people's hands.
university_explanation: The couplet plays two compounds against each other: urulaayam (உருளாயம், 'gain from what rolls', i.e. the die, கவறு) and porulaayam (பொருளாயம், 'wealth and its revenue'). Oovaadhu koorin (ஓவாது கூறின்) means 'if one ceaselessly calls', which Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar take as calling out the stake, while Solomon Pappaiah reads it as boasting of one's winnings. Pooip (போஒய், alapedai of போய்) purame padum says the wealth 'goes and lands outside', which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss as 'reaches the enemies' (பகைவர்). Pope's English ('If prince unceasing speak of nought but play') and his prose gloss follow the traditional Parimelazhagar reading, which takes the subject to be a king, in keeping with the chapter's place in Porutpaal. The text is identical on both base sites.

tamil:
சிறுமை பலசெய்து சீரழிக்கும் சூதின்
வறுமை தருவதொன்று இல்.
transliteration:
Sirumai palaseydhu seerazhikkum soodhin
varumai tharuvadhondru il.
current_meaning: Nothing brings poverty like gambling, which causes many miseries and destroys a person's good name.
elementary_explanation: Some bad habits make you a little poorer. Gambling is the champion of them all: it takes your money, gets you into trouble, and makes people stop trusting you.
university_explanation: Sirumai pala seydhu (சிறுமை பல செய்து) means 'causing many miseries' (Mu. Varadarasanar: துன்பம் பலவற்றையும்), though sirumai literally means 'smallness, meanness' and can also suggest degradation. Seer (சீர்) here is renown or good standing, glossed as புகழ் by all four commentators. The superlative construction soodhin ... ondru il ('there is nothing like gambling') makes gambling the paramount cause of varumai (வறுமை, poverty). Textual note: both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net print the verb as சீரழக்கும், but ytamizh's own transliteration ('seerazhikkum') and every gloss (கெடுக்கும், அழிக்கும்) support the standard சீரழிக்கும், so சீரழக்கும் looks like a shared typographical slip; this reading should be confirmed against a printed edition. Kesikan's gloss adds that gambling does this 'to those who love it' (தன்னை விரும்பியவருக்கு).

tamil:
கவறும் கழகமும் கையும் தருக்கி
இவறியார் இல்லாகி யார்.
transliteration:
Kavarum kazhagamum kaiyum tharukki
ivariyaar illaagi yaar.
current_meaning: Those who took pride in the dice, the gaming hall and their own skill of hand, and would not let them go, are the ones who have ended up with nothing.
elementary_explanation: Some people are very proud of being good at a game, and they love the place where it is played. But if that game is gambling and they never stop, Valluvar says, they finish with empty pockets, as many before them did.
university_explanation: The first line names gambling's three parts: kavaru (கவறு, the dice), kazhagam (கழகம், the gaming hall) and kai (கை, the hand, meaning dexterity in throwing). Tharukki (தருக்கி) means 'taking pride in', and ivariyaar (இவறியார்) means 'those who clung to, would not let go'. Illaagiyaar (இல்லாகியார்) is past tense: 'became people who have nothing'. Pope's English brings this out ('the men in other days who came to nought'), and Solomon Pappaiah adds that this 'has happened before too' (முன்பும் உண்டு), so the couplet appeals to historical examples. Kesikan reads it as 'those once wealthy and now destitute', and Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the parenthetical 'even though they had every wealth'. Kesikan's text on thirukkural.net prints the dice as சுவறு, apparently a misprint for கவறு; the couplet itself is identical on both sites.

tamil:
அகடாரார் அல்லல் உழப்பர்சூ தென்னும்
முகடியான் மூடப்பட் டார்.
transliteration:
Agadaaraar allal uzhapparsoo thennum
mugadiyaan moodappat taar.
current_meaning: Those swallowed up by the goddess of misfortune called gambling will never have their bellies filled and will suffer many sorrows.
elementary_explanation: Picture a big dark cloud named 'Bad Luck' that swallows people whole. Once it has you, you never get enough to eat and troubles keep coming. Valluvar says gambling is that cloud.
university_explanation: Mugadi (முகடி) is Misfortune personified, the goddess known in Tamil as Moodevi or Jyeshtha (மூதேவி), the inauspicious elder sister of Lakshmi. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss it as மூதேவி, and Pope's verse renders it 'Misfortune's other name'. Moodappattaar (மூடப்பட்டார்) means 'those covered or engulfed', which Mu. Varadarasanar renders as 'swallowed' (விழுங்கப்பட்டவர்). Agadaaraar (அகடாரார்) is 'those whose belly (அகடு) is never filled', and allal uzhappar means 'will toil in affliction'. Following Parimelazhagar's two-world reading, Kesikan and the Pope prose gloss take the second clause to mean suffering in the next world as well. Kesikan's text on thirukkural.net seems to drop the negation ('வயிறார உணவைப் பெறுவதுடன்'), which is likely a transcription slip. The couplet text matches on both sites.

tamil:
பழகிய செல்வமும் பண்பும் கெடுக்கும்
கழகத்துக் காலை புகின்.
transliteration:
Pazhagiya selvamum panbum kedukkum
kazhagaththuk kaalai pugin.
current_meaning: If a person's time is spent in the gaming hall, it destroys both the wealth that has come down to him and his good character.
elementary_explanation: Your grandparents may have saved a treasure for your family and taught you good manners. Valluvar says that hanging around a gambling house can waste both: the treasure is lost, and the good manners slowly disappear too.
university_explanation: Pazhagiya selvam (பழகிய செல்வம்) is 'long-familiar wealth', which all commentators take as ancestral or inherited property (Kalaignar: மூதாதையர் தேடிவைத்த சொத்து). Panbu (பண்பு) is good character or natural virtue. The second line contains an interpretive crux: kaalai (காலை) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Kalaignar and Kesikan as kaalam, 'time' ('if one's time is passed in the gaming hall'), and Kesikan adds 'the time meant for doing good'. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reads it literally as 'morning' ('if one goes to the gaming hall in the morning'), the hour that should belong to work. Kazhagam (கழகம்) also appears in 935 as the gaming place. The couplet is identical on both sites.

tamil:
பொருள்கெடுத்துப் பொய்மேற் கொளீஇ அருள்கெடுத்து
அல்லல் உழப்பிக்கும் சூது.
transliteration:
Porulkeduththup poimer koleei arulkeduththu
allal uzhappikkum soodhu.
current_meaning: Gambling destroys wealth, drives a person to lying, kills compassion, and makes him suffer in misery.
elementary_explanation: First gambling takes your money. Then you start fibbing to cover it up. Then you stop caring about other people. And at the end you are very unhappy. Valluvar lists these four steps like a staircase going down.
university_explanation: The couplet is a chain of four causative actions with gambling (soodhu, சூது) held back as the subject until the last word. Porul keduththu (பொருள்கெடுத்து) means 'ruining wealth'; poi mer koleei (பொய்மேற் கொளீஇ) means 'making one take up falsehood', where koleei is the causative alapedai form of kol ('take'); arul keduththu (அருள்கெடுத்து) means 'destroying compassion'. The last verb, uzhappikkum (உழப்பிக்கும், 'causes to toil in affliction'), is also causative. Arul, the compassion celebrated in Arattuppaal's chapter 25 (Aruludaimai), is the highest of the virtues lost. Kesikan follows the Parimelazhagar tradition in reading the misery as belonging to both worlds (இருமையும்), and the Pope prose gloss adds '(here and hereafter)'. Both base sites agree on the text.

tamil:
உடைசெல்வம் ஊண்ஒளி கல்விஎன்று ஐந்தும்
அடையாவாம் ஆயங் கொளின்.
transliteration:
Udaiselvam oon-oli kalvi-endru aindhum
adaiyaavaam aayang kolin.
current_meaning: If a person takes up gambling, these five will never reach him: clothing, wealth, food, renown and learning.
elementary_explanation: Think of five good things: clothes to wear, money, food, a good name, and learning. Valluvar says that if you make gambling your habit, all five walk away from you.
university_explanation: The couplet lists five goods: udai (உடை, clothing), selvam (செல்வம், wealth), oon (ஊண், food), oli (ஒளி, 'light', i.e. fame or renown) and kalvi (கல்வி, learning). Aayam (ஆயம்) here means gambling, and aayang kolin means 'if one takes it up'. Adaiyaavaam (அடையாவாம்) says these 'will not come to' him, so the stress is on goods that are never gained, not only goods lost. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kesikan list the five in reverse order (fame, learning, wealth, food, clothing), presumably following Parimelazhagar's ranking from highest to lowest, while Pope keeps the Kural's order. Kesikan adds 'even if one does it thinking it mere sport' (வேடிக்கை), and Sivayogi Sivakumar takes oli as 'self-knowledge'. The text is the same on both sites.

tamil:
இழத்தொறூஉம் காதலிக்கும் சூதேபோல் துன்பம்
உழத்தொறூஉம் காதற்று உயிர்.
transliteration:
Izhaththoruum kaadhalikkum soodhepol thunbam
uzhaththoruum kaadhatru uyir.
current_meaning: Just as gambling is loved all the more the more one loses at it, so the soul loves the body all the more the more it suffers.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever lost a game and immediately shouted, 'One more try!'? The more you lose, the more you want to play. Valluvar says life is like that too: even when it hurts, we hold on to it more tightly.
university_explanation: The closing couplet turns a psychological observation about gambling into a general statement about existence. Izhaththoruum (இழத்தொறூஉம்) and uzhaththoruum (உழத்தொறூஉம்), both with alapedai, mean 'every time one loses' and 'every time one suffers', placing loss and pain in parallel. Kaadhalikkum (காதலிக்கும், 'comes to love') and kaadhatru (காதற்று) carry the comparison. Most commentators (Mu. Varadarasanar, Kesikan, Pope) read kaadhatru as kaadhal + atru, 'has love, is fond': the soul (uyir) loves the body more as it suffers, just as the gambler loves gambling more as he loses. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh instead splits it as kaadhal + atru 'without love', giving the opposite sense that the soul does not love suffering, and adds that gambling can lead to despair. Pappaiah reverses which half is the comparison. The text is identical on both sites.

tamil:
மிகினும் குறையினும் நோய்செய்யும் நூலோர்
வளிமுதலா எண்ணிய மூன்று.
transliteration:
Miginum kuraiyinum noiseyyum noolor
valimudhalaa enniya moondru.
current_meaning: The three bodily forces that medical authors count, beginning with wind, cause disease whether they grow too strong or fall too low.
elementary_explanation: Think of a bicycle tyre: pump in too much air and it bursts, let out too much and it goes flat. Valluvar says the body has three such forces inside it, and it stays healthy only when each one is just right.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with theory before practice: noolor (நூலோர், 'the authors of the treatises') are the medical writers, and vali mudhalaa enniya moondru (வளிமுதலா எண்ணிய மூன்று, 'the three reckoned with wind first') are the three humours that Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all gloss as vaatham, piththam and silethumam (வாதம், பித்தம், சிலேத்துமம்), i.e. the vata-pitta-kapha triad of Ayurveda and Siddha medicine. The decisive words are miginum kuraiyinum (மிகினும் குறையினும், 'whether in excess or in deficiency'): illness is defined not as an invading thing but as loss of proportion. Following Parimelazhagar, Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan add that the humours are disturbed through a person's food and activity (உணவும் செயல்களும்), which is why the following couplets turn at once to eating. The chapter closes the Natpiyal section of Porutpaal in the traditional arrangement, a placement commentators explain by treating bodily health as the last of the things a ruler and householder must secure. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மருந்தென வேண்டாவாம் யாக்கைக்கு அருந்தியது
அற்றது போற்றி உணின்.
transliteration:
Marundhena vendaavaam yaakkaikku arundhiyadhu
atradhu potri unin.
current_meaning: The body needs nothing called medicine if a person eats only after making sure that what was eaten before has been fully digested.
elementary_explanation: You would not pour more water into a glass that is still full; it would spill everywhere. Valluvar says the stomach is like that glass: wait until it has finished the last meal before you fill it again, and you will hardly ever need a doctor.
university_explanation: The couplet makes a bold claim, that medicine (marundhu, மருந்து) becomes unnecessary (vendaavaam, வேண்டாவாம்) for the body (yaakkai, யாக்கை), on one condition: arundhiyadhu atradhu potri unin (அருந்தியது அற்றது போற்றி உணின்), 'if one eats after carefully confirming that what was taken has been digested'. Atradhu (அற்றது, literally 'that which has ceased') is the technical verb for complete digestion that recurs in 943 and 944. Potri (போற்றி) means not 'praising' here but 'observing with care'; Mu. Varadarasanar reads it as examining the state of digestion, and Kalaignar as allowing the proper interval between meals. Parimelazhagar's tradition reads the hyperbole as a statement of priority: prevention through regimen ranks above cure. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அற்றால் அறவறிந்து உண்க அஃதுடம்பு
பெற்றான் நெடிதுய்க்கும் ஆறு.
transliteration:
Atraal aravarindhu unga ahdhudambu
petraan nedidhuykkum aaru.
current_meaning: Once the previous meal is digested, eat knowing the right measure; that is how one who has received a body keeps it going for a long time.
elementary_explanation: A car runs far if you fill the tank properly and do not overflow it. Valluvar says your body is a gift you have been given, and eating the right amount at the right time is how you make it last a long, long time.
university_explanation: Atraal (அற்றால், 'when it has been digested') picks up the condition of 942, and adds aravarindhu (அறவறிந்து, அற + அறிந்து): Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read it as knowing the needed quantity, Puliyur Kesikan simply as eating in measure. The second line names the payoff: udambu petraan (உடம்பு பெற்றான், 'he who has obtained a body') can nedidhu uykkum (நெடிது உய்க்கும், 'carry it on long'). Kesikan glosses the body as 'this human frame so hard to obtain' (பெறுவதற்கரியதான இந்த மானிட யாக்கை), an Indian commonplace that human birth is rare and should not be wasted through gluttony. Parimelazhagar's line of interpretation thus links diet to longevity, not merely to comfort. Some editions print the first line as அற்றால் அளவறிந்து; ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net both read அறவறிந்து.

tamil:
அற்றது அறிந்து கடைப்பிடித்து மாறல்ல
துய்க்க துவரப் பசித்து.
transliteration:
Atradhu arindhu kadaippidiththu maaralla
thuykka thuvarap pasiththu.
current_meaning: Knowing that the earlier meal is digested, keep firmly to foods that agree with the body, and eat them only when truly hungry.
elementary_explanation: A plant needs water, but only when its soil has dried, and only clean water, not juice or soda. Valluvar says eat when you are really hungry, and choose the food that suits your body.
university_explanation: The couplet adds two refinements to the rule of digestion. Maaralla (மாறல்ல, 'things that are not contrary') are foods that do not disagree with one's constitution; Pappaiah extends this to foods unsuited to the body and to the season (உடம்பிற்கும் காலத்திற்கும் ஒவ்வாத). Kadaippidiththu (கடைப்பிடித்து) means holding firmly to such foods as a fixed practice. Thuvarap pasiththu (துவரப் பசித்து), 'being thoroughly hungry', makes real hunger, not appetite or habit, the signal to eat. Pope's translation renders the sense as 'when hunger prompteth thee, with constant care, the viands choose that well agree'. The idea of wholesome and unwholesome food relative to the person (Sanskrit satmya) is shared with Ayurveda, and the Parimelazhagar tradition reads the couplet as practical dietetics. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மாறுபாடு இல்லாத உண்டி மறுத்துண்ணின்
ஊறுபாடு இல்லை உயிர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Maarupaadu illaadha undi maruththunnin
oorupaadu illai uyirkku.
current_meaning: If one eats wholesome food and still holds back from eating too much of it, no harm comes to one's life.
elementary_explanation: Even your favourite ice cream will give you a tummy ache if you eat the whole tub. Valluvar says that even good food must be eaten with a 'no, that's enough' at the right moment.
university_explanation: Maarupaadu illaadha undi (மாறுபாடு இல்லாத உண்டி) is food that does not clash with the body, the same category as maaralla in 944. The key word is maruththu (மறுத்து, 'refusing'): Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read it as refusing more once the measure is reached, and Kesikan as eating not as the mind desires but only as much as causes no illness. Solomon Pappaiah takes a different line, reading maruththu as rejecting unsuitable foods, so that the couplet becomes about selection rather than quantity; this is a genuine interpretive divergence. Oorupaadu (ஊறுபாடு) is injury or harm, and uyirkku (உயிர்க்கு) 'to life' or 'to the soul dwelling in the body'. Parimelazhagar's reading, followed by most modern commentators, stresses restraint even with good food. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இழிவறிந்து உண்பான்கண் இன்பம்போல் நிற்கும்
கழிபேர் இரையான்கண் நோய்.
transliteration:
Izhivarindhu unbaankan inbampol nirkum
kazhiper iraiyaankan noi.
current_meaning: Just as well-being stays with the one who knows to eat a little less, so disease stays with the one who devours far too much.
elementary_explanation: Two friends go to a party. One eats until he is nicely full and goes home happy. The other stuffs himself and spends the night with a stomach ache. Valluvar says that is how it goes every time.
university_explanation: The couplet is a balanced antithesis. Izhivu (இழிவு) here means 'lessness': Varadarasanar glosses izhivarindhu unbaan as one who knows what the lesser measure is, and Kesikan as one who eats a little below the full measure; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it more morally as one who knows that taking more than needed is base, exploiting the word's other sense of 'meanness'. Inbam (இன்பம்) is well-being or pleasure, which nirkum (நிற்கும், 'stays, abides'). Kazhiper iraiyaan (கழிபேர் இரையான்) is a striking phrase: irai (இரை) is the word for an animal's prey or fodder, so the glutton is pictured as a beast gulping feed, and kazhiper (கழிபேர்) intensifies it to 'exceedingly great'. Disease abides with him as surely as health with the moderate eater. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தீயள வன்றித் தெரியான் பெரிதுண்ணின்
நோயள வின்றிப் படும்.
transliteration:
Theeyala vandrith theriyaan peridhunnin
noyala vindrip padum.
current_meaning: One who thoughtlessly eats a great deal, beyond the measure of the digestive fire, will suffer diseases beyond measure.
elementary_explanation: A small campfire can cook a small pot. If you pile a whole tree on it, the fire chokes and smoke goes everywhere. Valluvar says your tummy has a little fire too, and if you overload it, troubles pile up.
university_explanation: The couplet turns on a wordplay of measure: thee alavu (தீ அளவு, 'the measure of the fire') against noi alavu indri (நோய் அளவின்றி, 'diseases without measure'). The fire is the pasi-thee (பசித்தீ), the 'fire of hunger' or digestive fire, as Varadarasanar and Kesikan gloss it; it corresponds to the Ayurvedic jatharagni, whose strength determines how much food can be digested. Theriyaan (தெரியான்) is 'one who does not discern', and Kesikan adds that he ignores both the time and the quantity. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads thee alavu instead as an analogy to one who does not know how to use fire in measure, a minority reading. Parimelazhagar's tradition takes the metaphor medically, so that the couplet states a law: exceed the fire's measure and illness exceeds all measure. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நோய்நாடி நோய்முதல் நாடி அதுதணிக்கும்
வாய்நாடி வாய்ப்பச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Noinaadi noimudhal naadi adhuthanikkum
vaainaadi vaaippach cheyal.
current_meaning: Find out what the disease is, find out its cause, find out the way to relieve it, and then act in the way that fits.
elementary_explanation: When your bike makes a funny noise, a good mechanic first finds which part is wrong, then why it broke, then how to fix it, and only then gets out the tools. Valluvar says a good doctor does the same with a sick person.
university_explanation: The most quoted couplet of the chapter is built on a threefold naadi (நாடி, 'having examined'): the disease (noi), its root or first cause (noi mudhal, நோய் முதல்), and the means (vaai, வாய்) that will abate it (thanikkum, தணிக்கும்). Only then comes vaaippach cheyal (வாய்ப்பச் செயல்), 'act fittingly': Kesikan reads it as treating without error in procedure, Varadarasanar as in a way suited to the body. Commentators note the sequence of diagnosis, aetiology and therapy as a complete clinical method; Kalaignar adds that it applies to the ills of society as well as of the body. The repetition of naadi and of vaai/vaaippa gives the line a deliberate, step-by-step rhythm. The couplet appears in the sung version of the chapter by P. A. Muthukrishnan quoted on thirukkural.net. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உற்றான் அளவும் பிணியளவும் காலமும்
கற்றான் கருதிச் செயல்.
transliteration:
Utraan alavum piniyalavum kaalamum
katraan karudhich cheyal.
current_meaning: The learned physician should act only after weighing the patient's condition, the extent of the disease, and the time or season.
elementary_explanation: A baby and a grown-up with the same cold do not get the same dose of medicine. Valluvar says a good doctor thinks about who is sick, how sick they are, and what time it is before deciding what to do.
university_explanation: Three measures must be weighed: utraan alavu (உற்றான் அளவு), the measure of the one afflicted, which Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss as age and the like, and Kesikan as the patient's strength; pini alavu (பிணியளவு), the extent and nature of the disease; and kaalam (காலம்), which Sivayogi Sivakumar reads as the climate of the season, Kalaignar as the right time for treatment, and Pappaiah as both the duration of the illness and the time needed to cure it. The agent is katraan (கற்றான்), 'the one who has learned', i.e. the physician trained in the medical texts, and karudhi (கருதி) means 'having deliberated'. The couplet thus individualises treatment, echoing Ayurveda's attention to the patient's constitution and to season (ritu). Pope renders it 'the habitudes of patient and disease, the crises of the ill these must the learned leech think over well'. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உற்றவன் தீர்ப்பான் மருந்துழைச் செல்வானென்று
அப்பால் நாற்கூற்றே மருந்து.
transliteration:
Utravan theerppaan marundhuzhaich chelvaanendru
appaal naarkootre marundhu.
current_meaning: Medicine has four parts: the patient, the physician who cures, the remedy, and the one who stays at hand to prepare and give it.
elementary_explanation: Getting better is like a team game. The sick person must follow the plan, the doctor must know what to do, the medicine must be good, and someone like a parent or nurse must help every day. If one player is missing, the team struggles.
university_explanation: The chapter ends by defining medicine as naarkootru (நாற்கூற்று, 'fourfold'): utravan (உற்றவன், the one afflicted), theerppaan (தீர்ப்பான், the one who cures), marundhu (மருந்து, the remedy), and marundhuzhaich chelvaan (மருந்துழைச் செல்வான், literally 'he who goes near the medicine'). This last term divides the commentators: Varadarasanar reads it as the one who gives the medicine from close by, Kalaignar as the attendant at the bedside, Pappaiah and Kesikan as the preparer or compounder, and Pope's explanation as the compounder. The words appaal (அப்பால், 'that domain') and the closing marundhu frame the whole. Pope's gloss, following Parimelazhagar, adds that each of the four has four qualities in turn, sixteen in all. The fourfold scheme closely matches the Charaka Samhita's 'four feet' of therapy (physician, drug, attendant, patient), which is strong evidence that Valluvar knew the classical medical tradition. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இற்பிறந்தார் கண்அல்லது இல்லை இயல்பாகச்
செப்பமும் நாணும் ஒருங்கு.
transliteration:
Irpirandhaar kan alladhu illai iyalpaagach
cheppamum naanum orungu.
current_meaning: Rectitude and a sense of shame, found together and as second nature, are seen only in those born into a good family.
elementary_explanation: Some children say sorry and play fair without anyone telling them, because they have seen it at home every day. Valluvar says that fairness and feeling bad about doing wrong come most naturally to people who grew up in a good home.
university_explanation: The chapter opens the Kudiyiyal (குடியியல், the section on the citizen and his family) of Porutpal, and its first couplet sets the theme: kudimai (குடிமை) is the character that a good lineage (இல், 'house', hence family) is expected to carry. Cheppam (செப்பம்) is glossed by Mu. Varadarasanar as நடுவு நிலைமை, 'impartiality, rectitude', and by Solomon Pappaiah as purity of mind, word and deed; naanum (நாணும்) is shame or modesty, the recoil from what is unworthy. The force lies in iyalpaaga (இயல்பாக, 'by nature') and orungu (ஒருங்கு, 'together'): others may show one quality by effort, but the high-born show both effortlessly. Kalaignar's modern gloss reverses the direction, saying that only those who possess these qualities may be counted high-born, an egalitarian reading of a couplet that the medieval commentarial tradition read more literally. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஒழுக்கமும் வாய்மையும் நாணும்இம் மூன்றும்
இழுக்கார் குடிப்பிறந் தார்.
transliteration:
Ozhukkamum vaaymaiyum naanum im moondrum
izhukkaar kudippirandhaar.
current_meaning: Those born into a good family never slip from these three: right conduct, truthfulness and a sense of shame.
elementary_explanation: Think of a three-legged stool: good behaviour, telling the truth, and feeling bad about doing wrong. If one leg breaks, the stool falls. Valluvar says people from a good family keep all three legs strong.
university_explanation: The couplet names a triad: ozhukkam (ஒழுக்கம், right conduct, the subject of chapter 14), vaaymai (வாய்மை, truthfulness, chapter 30) and naan (நாண், shame, which will receive its own chapter, 102). The verb izhukkaar (இழுக்கார்) means 'they do not slip or lapse', so the claim is about steadiness over a lifetime, not occasional virtue. Mu. Varadarasanar adds that the well-born live in the right path 'by nature' (இயல்பாகவே), linking this couplet to the iyalpaaga of 951, while Kalaignar again turns it into a definition: only those who never lapse in these three are to be counted high-born, and he glosses naan as maanam (மானம், honour). The word division நாணும்இம் மூன்றும் (naanum im moondrum, 'shame, these three') appears in both ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நகைஈகை இன்சொல் இகழாமை நான்கும்
வகையென்ப வாய்மைக் குடிக்கு.
transliteration:
Nagai eegai insol igazhaamai naangum
vagaiyenba vaaymaik kudikku.
current_meaning: A cheerful face, generosity, kind words and never belittling others: these four, the wise say, are the marks of a truly noble family.
elementary_explanation: When a friend visits, a kind family smiles, shares their snacks, speaks nicely and never makes fun of anyone. Valluvar says those four habits show you what a truly good family looks like.
university_explanation: The couplet lists four marks (naangum, நான்கும்): nagai (நகை, a smiling or cheerful countenance), eegai (ஈகை, giving, the subject of chapter 23), insol (இன்சொல், pleasant speech, chapter 10) and igazhaamai (இகழாமை, not scorning or belittling). Vaaymaik kudi (வாய்மைக் குடி) means a family that is genuinely, not nominally, noble; Puliyur Kesikan reads it as a lineage that never changes its character, and he applies the four marks especially to one's conduct towards the poor. Vagai (வகை) is 'kind' or 'proper quality', and enba (என்ப, 'they say') marks the list as received wisdom. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அடுக்கிய கோடி பெறினும் குடிப்பிறந்தார்
குன்றுவ செய்தல் இலர்.
transliteration:
Adukkiya kodi perinum kudippirandhaar
kundruva seydhal ilar.
current_meaning: Even if they could gain crores upon crores, the nobly born will not do anything that lowers their family's worth.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone offers you a giant pile of money if you will just cheat once. A person from a good family says no, because no pile of money is worth losing their good name.
university_explanation: Adukkiya kodi (அடுக்கிய கோடி) is 'crores stacked one upon another', hyperbole for limitless wealth, and perinum (பெறினும், 'even if they obtain') concedes the strongest temptation. Kundruva (குன்றுவ) are acts that diminish, literally 'that make small', and the commentators unanimously take the diminished thing to be the family's honour: Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of faults that would lower the family's distinction, and Kalaignar of deeds that would spoil that excellence. The couplet thus sets the chapter's characteristic contrast between wealth (Porul) and the inherited good name that the section on family (Kudiyiyal) values above it. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
வழங்குவ துள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும் பழங்குடி
பண்பில் தலைப்பிரிதல் இன்று.
transliteration:
Vazhanguvadhu ulveezhndhak kannum pazhangudi
panbil thalaippiridhal indru.
current_meaning: Even when their means for giving have shrunk, those of an old and worthy family never part from their generous character.
elementary_explanation: A grandmother who used to cook big meals for everyone now has only a little rice, but she still shares it with a hungry neighbour. Valluvar says that is how people from a good old family act: they keep giving even when they have little.
university_explanation: Vazhanguvadhu (வழங்குவது) is 'that which is given', and ulveezhndha (உள்வீழ்ந்த) means 'fallen inward, shrunk', so the opening line pictures the family's power of giving contracting through poverty; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as the capacity to give having dwindled through want. Pazhangudi (பழங்குடி) is 'the ancient family', the old line whose character is long established, and thalaippiridhal (தலைப்பிரிதல்) means 'to separate from', here from their panbu (பண்பு, nature, especially the generous disposition). Sivayogi Sivakumar and Solomon Pappaiah both specify that it is the giving nature that endures, while Kalaignar explicitly names poverty as the blow. Both sites print the words as வழங்குவ துள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும், a traditional metrical division of வழங்குவது உள்வீழ்ந்தக் கண்ணும்.

tamil:
சலம்பற்றிச் சால்பில செய்யார்மா சற்ற
குலம்பற்றி வாழ்தும்என் பார்.
transliteration:
Salampatrich chaalbila seyyaar maasatra
kulampatri vaazhdhum enbaar.
current_meaning: Those who resolve to live true to their spotless family line will never stoop to deceit or do anything unworthy.
elementary_explanation: If your family has always been known for honesty, you think, 'I will not be the one who spoils our name.' So you do not cheat, even when it would be easy.
university_explanation: Salam (சலம்) means deceit or crookedness, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render as vanchanai (வஞ்சனை); chaalbila (சால்பில) are acts lacking saalbu (சால்பு, worthiness, nobility of character, the subject of chapter 99). Maasatra kulam (மாசற்ற குலம்) is 'a family free of stain', and vaazhdhum enbaar (வாழ்தும் என்பார்) are 'those who say, we shall live (by it)', so the couplet describes a conscious resolve to keep faith with an unblemished line. Solomon Pappaiah adds 'even when poverty comes', reading the couplet as continuing the thought of 955 that hardship tests the well-born. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net, both dividing the line as மா சற்ற / மாசற்ற across the metrical break.

tamil:
குடிப்பிறந்தார் கண்விளங்கும் குற்றம் விசும்பின்
மதிக்கண் மறுப்போல் உயர்ந்து.
transliteration:
Kudippirandhaar kan vilangum kutram visumbin
madhikkan maruppol uyarndhu.
current_meaning: A fault in someone of good birth stands out for all to see, like the dark spot on the moon high in the sky.
elementary_explanation: A tiny ink spot on a dirty shirt is hard to see, but the same spot on a bright white shirt is easy to notice. Valluvar says that a small mistake by someone from a respected family shows up just like that spot.
university_explanation: The simile is visumbin madhikkan maru (விசும்பின் மதிக்கண் மறு), 'the blemish on the moon in the sky'; maru (மறு) is a spot or stain, which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as kalangam (களங்கம்). Uyarndhu (உயர்ந்து, 'being high, raised up') does double work: the moon is high in the sky, and the well-born are high in society, so their flaws are exposed to everyone. Puliyur Kesikan adds that the fault may be small in size yet known to the whole world, and Kalaignar notes that it shows 'without any concealment'. Sivayogi Sivakumar's gloss reads the image as the full moon itself, but the standard commentators understand the dark mark on its face. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நலத்தின்கண் நாரின்மை தோன்றின் அவனைக்
குலத்தின்கண் ஐயப் படும்.
transliteration:
Nalaththinkan naarinmai thondrin avanaik
kulaththinkan aiyap padum.
current_meaning: If a lack of love shows up in someone who seems good, people will begin to doubt that he really comes from the family he claims.
