elementary_explanation: If a boy from a famously kind family is mean to a puppy, people say, 'Is he really from that kind family?' Valluvar says that being unkind makes others wonder where you came from.
university_explanation: Naar (நார்) is literally 'fibre', the tough strand that binds, and by extension affection or love; naarinmai (நாரின்மை) is the want of it, which Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan gloss as anbu-inmai or arul-inmai, lack of love or compassion. The opening word nalam (நலம்) is read in several ways: Mu. Varadarasanar takes it as one's good qualities, Puliyur Kesikan as the family's distinction, and Kalaignar as beauty and renown. Aiyap padum (ஐயப் படும், 'will be doubted') makes the striking claim that conduct can call ancestry itself into question, which is the hinge between this chapter's praise of lineage and the ethical reading that says character, not birth, is the real proof. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை கால்காட்டும் காட்டும்
குலத்தில் பிறந்தார்வாய்ச் சொல்.
transliteration:
Nilaththil kidandhamai kaal kaattum kaattum
kulaththil pirandhaarvaaich chol.
current_meaning: Just as a sprout shows the nature of the soil it grew in, a person's words show the family they come from.
elementary_explanation: A healthy green plant tells you the soil is good. In the same way, when someone speaks kindly and wisely, you can tell they grew up in a good home.
university_explanation: The image is agricultural: kaal (கால்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan as mulai (முளை), the sprout or shoot, which reveals (kaattum, காட்டும்) what lay hidden in the soil (nilaththil kidandhamai, நிலத்தில் கிடந்தமை). Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar widen it to the crop that grows there. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads kaal in its common sense of 'foot', so that the soil clinging to one's feet shows where one has walked; this is a minority reading that the standard commentators do not follow. The repetition kaattum kaattum (காட்டும் காட்டும்) closes the simile and opens its application: so too the speech (vaaich chol, வாய்ச்சொல்) of those born in a family reveals that family. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நலம்வேண்டின் நாணுடைமை வேண்டும் குலம்வேண்டின்
வேண்டுக யார்க்கும் பணிவு.
transliteration:
Nalamvendin naanudaimai vendum kulamvendin
venduga yaarkkum panivu.
current_meaning: If you want goodness, you must have a sense of shame; if you want a noble family name, you must be humble towards everyone.
elementary_explanation: Kids who say 'I'm the best!' all the time do not get respect. Kids who are polite to everyone, even the youngest, do. Valluvar says that if you want your family to be respected, be humble with everyone.
university_explanation: The closing couplet turns the chapter from description to instruction with a double condition built on the verb vendu (வேண்டு, 'to want, to require'): nalam vendin (நலம் வேண்டின், 'if you want good') requires naanudaimai (நாணுடைமை, the possession of shame), and kulam vendin (குலம் வேண்டின், 'if you want family standing') requires panivu (பணிவு, humility) towards yaarkkum (யார்க்கும், everyone). Puliyur Kesikan specifies shame at blame (பழிக்கு நாணம்), and Kalaignar adds 'without arrogance' (ஆணவமின்றி). The effect is to make lineage something earned and maintained by humility rather than simply inherited, which ties the chapter's ending back to the 'by nature' of 951. Naanudaimai is also the title of chapter 102, and the two chapters are often read together. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்றி அமையாச் சிறப்பின ஆயினும்
குன்ற வருப விடல்.
transliteration:
Indri amaiyaach chirappina aayinum
Kundra varupa vidal.
current_meaning: Even if certain acts are so important that life seems impossible without them, give them up if doing them would lower your dignity and the honour of your family.
elementary_explanation: Imagine you could win the biggest prize at school, but only by copying someone else's answers. The prize feels like something you cannot live without, but this kural says: if getting it makes you smaller inside, walk away from it.
university_explanation: The chapter on maanam (மானம், honour, self-respect) follows Kudimai (Nobility of Family) and is read in the Parimelazhagar tradition as the quality of never sinking below one's station. The opening couplet sets the bar at its highest: indri amaiyaa (இன்றி அமையா, 'that without which one cannot exist') describes acts that seem indispensable, and kundra varupa (குன்ற வருப) are acts that bring about a 'lowering' (kundru, to diminish), which must be let go (vidal, விடல்). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan both gloss the lowering as a fall in kudi-p-perumai (the honour of one's lineage), tying the chapter to the preceding one; Kalaignar generalises it to one's own dignity. The Pope translation quoted on ytamizh.com renders it 'Reject each act that may thine honour's clearness stain.' The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சீரினும் சீரல்ல செய்யாரே சீரொடு
பேராண்மை வேண்டு பவர்.
transliteration:
Seerinum seeralla seyyaare seerodu
Peraanmai vendu pavar.
current_meaning: Those who want both fame and true nobility will not do anything unworthy, even if it would win them fame.
elementary_explanation: Some people will do anything to become famous, even mean or silly things. This kural says that people who want to be both well-known and truly good will never do something shameful just to get noticed.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on seer (சீர், renown, excellence): seerinum (சீரினும், 'even for renown') and seeralla (சீரல்ல, 'what is not excellent', unworthy deeds). Those who desire seerodu peraanmai (சீரொடு பேராண்மை), renown together with great 'manliness' or nobility of spirit, do not do such things. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses peraanmai as பெரிய ஆண்மை and the unworthy acts as those unfit for kudi-p-perumai (family honour); Kalaignar reads it as a heroic life that will not chase fame by acts contrary to self-respect. The point sharpens the previous kural: not only necessity but even fame itself cannot justify a lowering act. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெருக்கத்து வேண்டும் பணிதல் சிறிய
சுருக்கத்து வேண்டும் உயர்வு.
transliteration:
Perukkaththu vendum panidhal siriya
Surukkaththu vendum uyarvu.
current_meaning: When fortune swells, be humble; when it shrinks to little, hold your head high.
elementary_explanation: When you win a game, it is good to be kind and not show off. When you lose, it is good to stand tall and not beg or sulk. This kural says to bow a little in good times and stand straight in hard times.
university_explanation: A perfectly balanced antithesis: perukkam (பெருக்கம், increase, prosperity) is set against surukkam (சுருக்கம், contraction, want), and panidhal (பணிதல், bending, humility) against uyarvu (உயர்வு, height, unbending dignity). Siriya (சிறிய, 'small') intensifies the second half: in a narrow, reduced state. Mu. Varadarasanar reads uyarvu as 'height that does not bow' (பணியாத உயர்வு), and Solomon Pappaiah as not stooping to others in poverty. Maanam here is not pride but a discipline that runs against circumstance: humble when one could afford arrogance, upright when one is tempted to grovel. Pope's version on ytamizh.com: 'Bow down thy soul, with increase blest, in happy hour; / Lift up thy heart, when stript of all by fortune's power.' Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
தலையின் இழிந்த மயிரனையர் மாந்தர்
நிலையின் இழிந்தக் கடை.
transliteration:
Thalaiyin izhindha mayiranaiyar maandhar
Nilaiyin izhindhak kadai.
current_meaning: People who fall from their honourable position become like hair that has fallen from the head: once valued, now worthless.
elementary_explanation: Hair on your head is combed and cared for. But once a hair falls on the floor, nobody wants it. This kural says a person who drops their good behaviour and self-respect loses the respect others gave them, just like that fallen hair.
university_explanation: The simile works through a single verb, izhi (இழி, to descend, fall, be debased), used twice: hair izhindha from the head (fallen) and people izhindha from their nilai (நிலை, station, standing). On the head, hair is an ornament; once fallen it is swept away. Mu. Varadarasanar reads thalai as both 'head' and 'high place' (தலைமை), so the image doubles as falling from leadership. The Parimelazhagar tradition places this after 963 to show what happens when the discipline of maanam fails. Kalaignar applies it to someone who held a high place in people's hearts. Pope: 'Like hairs from off the head that fall to earth, / When fall'n from high estate are men of noble birth.' Both online texts read இழிந்தக் கடை.

tamil:
குன்றின் அனையாரும் குன்றுவர் குன்றுவ
குன்றி அனைய செயின்.
transliteration:
Kundrin anaiyaarum kundruvar kundruva
Kundri anaiya seyin.
current_meaning: Even people as great as a mountain are brought low if they do something debasing, even something as small as a kunri seed.
elementary_explanation: A big, beautiful glass of milk can be spoiled by one tiny drop of ink. This kural says even a very great person can lose respect by doing one small mean thing.
university_explanation: A celebrated piece of wordplay on the root kundru (குன்று): kundru as noun means 'hill' (kundrin anaiyaar, those like a hill), as verb 'to diminish' (kundruvar, they will be lowered), kundruva are 'diminishing' (debasing) acts, and kundri (குன்றி) is the kunrimani, the small red-and-black seed of Abrus precatorius used as a jeweller's weight. The contrast of hill and seed sets the scale: the smallest dishonour outweighs the largest standing. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both read kundri anaiya as 'even a kunrimani's weight'. Pope keeps the botanical sense: 'If meanness, slight as abrus grain, by men be wrought.' Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
புகழ்இன்றால் புத்தேள்நாட்டு உய்யாதால் என்மற்று
இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை.
transliteration:
Pugazhindraal puththelnaattu uyyaadhaal enmatru
Ikazhvaarpin sendru nilai.
current_meaning: Following and fawning on those who despise you brings no fame in this world and no place in heaven; what then is it good for?
elementary_explanation: Some children follow around a bully who laughs at them, hoping to be liked. This kural asks: what do you get from that? Nobody admires it, and it does not make you a better person. Better to keep your self-respect.
university_explanation: The couplet is a rhetorical question built on the two goods of classical Tamil ethics: pugazh (புகழ், fame in this world) and puththel naadu (புத்தேள் நாடு, the land of the gods, i.e. heaven, reward in the next). Ikazhvaar pin sendru nilai (இகழ்வார்பின் சென்று நிலை), 'the state of going after those who scorn one', yields neither, hence en matru (என்மற்று), 'what else then?'. Solomon Pappaiah reads it as abandoning honour in order to live by following one's despisers. Kalaignar's gloss pointedly adds 'a heaven that does not exist', a modern rationalist reading; the older commentators take heaven at face value. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
ஒட்டார்பின் சென்றொருவன் வாழ்தலின் அந்நிலையே
கெட்டான் எனப்படுதல் நன்று.
transliteration:
Ottaarpin sendroruvan vaazhdhalin annilaiye
Kettaan enappadudhal nandru.
current_meaning: It is better to be spoken of as ruined, standing firm in one's own condition, than to make a living by trailing after those who do not value you.
elementary_explanation: Imagine choosing between staying poor but proud, or getting treats every day by doing whatever an unkind person tells you. This kural says it is better to lose the treats and keep your self-respect.
university_explanation: Ottaar (ஒட்டார்) are those who do not 'stick' to one: people who do not regard or accept one, or enemies. Living by following them (pin sendru vaazhdhal) is set against being called kettaan (கெட்டான், 'he is ruined', or 'he perished'). The phrase annilaiye (அந்நிலையே), 'in that very state', is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as remaining in one's own condition without stooping, while Puliyur Kesikan, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take kettaan more starkly as 'died'. Pope's English, quoted on ytamizh.com, follows the stronger reading: 'Better 'twere said, He's perished! than to gain / The means to live, following in foeman's train.' The couplet expresses a priority of honour over comfort, not an instruction to seek death. Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
மருந்தோமற்று ஊன்ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை பெருந்தகைமை
பீடழிய வந்த இடத்து.
transliteration:
Marundhomatru oonombum vaazhkkai perundhagaimai
Peedazhiya vandha idaththu.
current_meaning: When one's greatness and dignity are being destroyed, is a life that merely keeps the body going a medicine against death?
elementary_explanation: Everyone grows old one day, no matter what. This kural asks: if you will not live forever anyway, why trade away your good name just to stay comfortable a little longer?
university_explanation: The rhetorical question marundho (மருந்தோ, 'is it a medicine?') implies a medicine against death (saavaamai, deathlessness), as Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both supply. Oon ombum vaazhkkai (ஊன் ஓம்பும் வாழ்க்கை) is a life that merely 'nourishes the flesh', set against perundhagaimai (பெருந்தகைமை, nobility) and peedu (பீடு, dignity, greatness), whose destruction is the occasion. The argument is that since death cannot be escaped, saving the body at the cost of honour gains nothing lasting. Kalaignar makes this explicit: there is no medicine for not dying, so do not lower your worth for a better life. Text identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (some editions divide it மருந்தோமற் றூனோம்பும்).

tamil:
மயிர்நீப்பின் வாழாக் கவரிமா அன்னார்
உயிர்நீப்பர் மானம் வரின்.
transliteration:
Mayirneeppin vaazhaak kavarimaa annaar
Uyirneeppar maanam varin.
current_meaning: Like the yak said not to survive the loss of its hair, people of honour would give up life itself rather than live when their honour is taken from them.
elementary_explanation: An old story says the yak loves its long, beautiful hair so much it cannot live without it. This kural uses that story to say that some people treasure their good name the way the yak treasures its hair: nothing is worth losing it for.
university_explanation: The kavarimaa (கவரிமா) is the yak (Bos grunniens), whose tail-hair was prized for the chowrie or royal fly-whisk (chamara); popular Tamil usage later turned it into 'kavarimaan', a deer, though commentators identify it as the yak. The belief that it dies on losing its hair is poetic convention, not natural history; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as losing all its hair. Maanam varin (மானம் வரின்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar as 'if honour is about to be destroyed'. The Parimelazhagar tradition sees here the culmination of the chapter: honour valued above life. This is classical heroic ethics and should be read historically, as a statement of honour's supreme worth, not as a recommendation to end one's life; several traditions compared below explicitly reject taking one's own life. Text identical on both sources; Pope: 'Like the wild ox that, of its tuft bereft, will pine away.'

tamil:
இளிவரின் வாழாத மானம் உடையார்
ஒளிதொழுது ஏத்தும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Ilivarin vaazhaadha maanam udaiyaar
Olidhozhudhu eththum ulagu.
current_meaning: The world forever bows to and praises the glory of honourable people who would not go on living in disgrace.
elementary_explanation: People remember and admire heroes who never gave up doing what was right, even when it was very hard. This kural says the whole world keeps honouring such people long after they are gone.
university_explanation: Ilivu (இளிவு) is disgrace, humiliation; ilivarin vaazhaadha (இளிவரின் வாழாத) are those who 'do not live on when disgrace comes'. Oli (ஒளி), literally 'light', here means radiant fame, the glory that survives a person; Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan gloss it as pugazh (புகழ்) or pugazh vadivu (the form of one's fame). Thozhudhu eththum (தொழுது ஏத்தும்) is the language of worship: folding hands and praising. The chapter closes where Tamil heroic ethics often closes, with lasting fame as the reward of honour. Read today, its lasting point is that the world reveres those who keep their integrity at great cost. Pope: 'Who, when dishonour comes, refuse to live, their honoured memory / Will live in worship and applause of all the world for aye!' Text identical on both sources.

tamil:
ஒளிஒருவற்கு உள்ள வெறுக்கை இளிஒருவற்கு
அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்.
transliteration:
Olioruvarku ulla verukkai ilioruvarku
ahdhirandhu vaazhdhum enal.
current_meaning: A person's shining glory is an abundance of inner drive; a person's disgrace is the thought, 'I will get through life without it.'
elementary_explanation: Some kids say, 'I will try the hard puzzle!' and their faces light up. Others say, 'I'll just skip it and sit.' Valluvar says the first kind of heart is what makes a person shine, and the lazy 'I'll just skip it' is what makes a person small.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by defining greatness as an inner quality rather than a rank: oli (ஒளி, 'light, lustre, renown') is ulla verukkai (உள்ள வெறுக்கை), literally 'the wealth/abundance of the mind', which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses as ஊக்கமிகுதி ('excess of zeal') and Puliyur Kesikan, following the older commentarial line descending from Parimelazhagar, as the resolve 'I will do what others find hard to do'. Its opposite, ili (இளி, 'disgrace'), is not failure but the attitude ahdhirandhu vaazhdhum enal (அஃதிறந்து வாழ்தும் எனல்), 'saying we shall live having let it go'. Pope's 'The light of life is mental energy' follows the majority reading; Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reads verukkai as வெறுமை ('emptiness of mind'), a contemplative minority interpretation not shared by the classical glosses. Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Maanam (Honour, ch. 97), the chapter moves from guarding one's dignity to the active, self-effacing greatness of the noble. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பிறப்பொக்கும் எல்லா உயிர்க்கும் சிறப்பொவ்வா
செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமை யான்.
transliteration:
Pirappokkum ellaa uyirkkum sirappovvaa
seydhozhil vetrumai yaan.
current_meaning: All living beings are alike in birth; distinction differs only because of the difference in the deeds they do.
elementary_explanation: Every baby is born the same way, crying and tiny, whether in a palace or a hut. What makes people different later is what they choose to do: who helps, who works hard, who is kind. That is where real specialness comes from.
university_explanation: The couplet sets piRappu (பிறப்பு, 'birth') against siRappu (சிறப்பு, 'distinction'): the first ஒக்கும் ('is equal') for all, the second ஒவ்வா ('is not equal') because of seydhozhil vetrumai (செய்தொழில் வேற்றுமை, 'difference in the work done'). Commentators differ on the scope of uyir: Puliyur Kesikan restricts it to 'all human lives' (எல்லா மக்களுயிர்க்கும்), the older reading, while modern glosses keep 'all living beings'. They also differ on tozhil: Mu. Varadarasanar speaks of the high and low grades of occupations, whereas Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar read it as one's deeds or skill and make the verse an explicit statement that all are equal by birth. This egalitarian reading has made the couplet one of the most frequently cited in modern Tamil debates on caste. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
மேலிருந்தும் மேலல்லார் மேலல்லர் கீழிருந்தும்
கீழல்லார் கீழல் லவர்.
transliteration:
Melirundhum melallaar melallar keezhirundhum
keezhallaar keezhal lavar.
current_meaning: Those who are not truly high are not high even when they sit high; those who are not base are not low even when they are placed low.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a bully sitting on the tallest chair in class, and a kind child sitting on the floor. The tall chair does not make the bully great, and the floor does not make the kind child small. Who you are matters more than where you sit.
university_explanation: The verse is a chiasmus built on mel (மேல், 'above, superior') and keezh (கீழ், 'below, base'), each used both for physical or social position and for moral quality: melirundhum melallaar melallar, 'though they be above, those not superior are not superior'. Puliyur Kesikan makes the image literal, 'though they sit on high seats' (உயர்ந்த ஆசனங்களிலே), and ties superiority to having done 'deeds hard to do', linking back to Kural 971; Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar render mel as high office or position. Pope's 'men of lofty line' reads it as birth, which carries the theme on from Kural 972. The repeated negatives (அல்லார், அல்லர், அல்லவர்) give the couplet its characteristic Valluvan density. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஒருமை மகளிரே போலப் பெருமையும்
தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின் உண்டு.
transliteration:
Orumai magalire polap perumaiyum
thannaiththaan kondozhugin undu.
current_meaning: Like a woman of single-hearted faithfulness, greatness too exists only for the one who guards himself.
elementary_explanation: A promise only stays a promise if you keep it, even when nobody is watching. Valluvar says greatness is the same: it is not a prize someone hands you, it stays with you only while you keep guarding your own good behaviour.
university_explanation: The simile turns on orumai magalir (ஒருமை மகளிர், 'women of oneness'), which the commentators uniformly read as women of undivided chastity (கற்பு, karpu): Mu. Varadarasanar says ஒரு தன்மையான கற்புடைய மகளிர், and Puliyur Kesikan describes women whose minds do not waver and who guard themselves without lapsing. The point of comparison is thannaiththaan kondozhugin (தன்னைத்தான் கொண்டொழுகின், 'if one conducts oneself holding oneself'), that is, self-guarding: greatness, like chastity, cannot be imposed from outside and is lost by a single lapse. The gendered simile reflects the period; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it more inwardly as being true to oneself. Pope's 'Like single-hearted women, greatness too, / Exists while to itself is true' keeps the ambiguity. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெருமை யுடையவர் ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றின்
அருமை உடைய செயல்.
transliteration:
Perumai yudaiyavar aatruvaar aatrin
arumai udaiya seyal.
current_meaning: Those who have greatness will accomplish, in the proper way, deeds that are hard for others to do.
elementary_explanation: Some jobs are so hard that most people give up, like building a tall tower of blocks without it falling. A great person keeps going and does it carefully, the right way, until it stands.
university_explanation: The verse plays on aatru (ஆற்று), used twice: aatruvaar ('they will accomplish') and aatrin, which commentators take either as 'by the (proper) way' (ஆறு, 'path, method') or as 'if they set about it'. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read the first: 'in the way proper to it' (உரிய நெறியில்). Puliyur Kesikan adds 'even when they have fallen into poverty' (வறுமையான போதும்), the traditional gloss also reflected in Pope's explanation '(Though reduced) the great will be able to perform…', which holds that greatness shows itself in rare deeds even without resources. The couplet makes concrete the 'deeds hard for others' that Kural 971 called the light of a person. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சிறியார் உணர்ச்சியுள் இல்லை பெரியாரைப்
பேணிக்கொள் வேமென்னும் நோக்கு.
transliteration:
Siriyaar unarchchiyul illai periyaaraip
penikkol vemennum nokku.
current_meaning: The aim 'Let us cherish the great and make their way our own' does not arise in the minds of small-minded people.
elementary_explanation: When a great teacher comes to school, some children run to listen and learn, hoping to become like her. Others just shrug and keep playing. Valluvar says wanting to learn from great people is itself a sign of a big heart.
university_explanation: Siriyaar (சிறியார், 'the small') is the counter-term to periyaar (பெரியார், 'the great') throughout this chapter and the next. The key phrase is peNikkoLvem (பேணிக்கொள்வேம், 'we will cherish and take to ourselves'): Puliyur Kesikan reads it as 'we will serve the great and attain their nature ourselves' (அவரியல்பை நாமும் அடைவோம்), Solomon Pappaiah as following them and preserving their tradition, and Mu. Varadarasanar as honouring them, which the small cannot do because they do not perceive the greatness at all. Nokku (நோக்கு, 'aim, outlook') and unarchchi (உணர்ச்சி, 'feeling, awareness') make the point psychological: the lack is in perception, not merely in will. Pope renders 'As votaries of the truly great we will ourselves enroll'. The text matches on both sites, with ytamizh omitting the final full stop.

tamil:
இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்றாம் சிறப்புந்தான்
சீரல் லவர்கண் படின்.
transliteration:
Irappe purindha thozhitraam sirappundhaan
seeral lavarkan padin.
current_meaning: Even distinction, when it falls to unworthy people, turns into deeds that overstep every limit.
elementary_explanation: Give a bossy child the job of class leader and he might start ordering everyone around and showing off. The badge was meant for helping, but in the wrong hands it turns into bullying.
university_explanation: Sirappu (சிறப்பு, 'eminence, distinction') here covers whatever raises a person; Solomon Pappaiah lists money, learning and office, and Pope's explanation 'nobility of birth, wealth and learning' reflects the traditional commentarial list. When it reaches seeral lavar (சீரல்லவர், 'those without worth'), it becomes irappe purindha thozhitru (இறப்பே புரிந்த தொழிற்று), 'of the nature of acting only in excess': irappu (இறப்பு) is taken by Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar as 'overstepping the bounds' (வரம்பு மீறிய செயல்) and by Kesikan as being driven into arrogance. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads irappu as 'destruction', a minority gloss. The couplet is the negative counterpart to Kural 975: the same eminence that lets the great do rare deeds makes the small insolent. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பணியுமாம் என்றும் பெருமை சிறுமை
அணியுமாம் தன்னை வியந்து.
transliteration:
Paniyumaam endrum perumai sirumai
aniyumaam thannai viyandhu.
current_meaning: Greatness always bows in humility; littleness decks itself out, marvelling at itself.
elementary_explanation: A tree heavy with fruit bends its branches low, while an empty stalk sticks straight up. Valluvar says truly great people are like the fruit tree: they stay humble, while small people keep showing off.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two verbs in parallel, paniyum (பணியும், 'bends, submits') and aniyum (அணியும், 'adorns'), with the expletive -aam (ஆம்) giving the tone of a settled maxim and endrum (என்றும், 'always') applying to both. Thannai viyandhu (தன்னை வியந்து, 'admiring itself') explains the adorning: littleness dresses itself up in its own praise. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'greatness walks in humility at all times, littleness praises itself', and Kalaignar adds that the small lie puffed up (இறுமாந்து). Pope's 'Greatness humbly bends, but littleness always / Spreads out its plumes' turns aniyum into a peacock image not in the Tamil. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பெருமை பெருமிதம் இன்மை சிறுமை
பெருமிதம் ஊர்ந்து விடல்.
transliteration:
Perumai perumidham inmai sirumai
perumidham oorndhu vidal.
current_meaning: Greatness is the absence of arrogance; littleness is to ride on arrogance all the way.
elementary_explanation: A real champion says, 'Thanks, my team helped me.' Someone who isn't much of a champion struts around shouting, 'I'm the best!' Valluvar says being great means not puffing yourself up at all.
university_explanation: The couplet defines both terms through a single word, perumidham (பெருமிதம், 'swagger, pride'), which etymologically contains the same peru- ('great') as perumai: greatness is its absence (inmai, இன்மை), littleness is perumidham oorndhu vidal (பெருமிதம் ஊர்ந்து விடல்), 'mounting and riding on pride'. Mu. Varadarasanar reads oorndhu vidal as 'pride growing until it reaches its limit and stopping there', while Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the contrast: having cause for pride yet not being proud is greatness, being proud without cause is littleness. Pope's 'Riding on car of vanity supreme' keeps the image of mounting a vehicle. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அற்றம் மறைக்கும் பெருமை சிறுமைதான்
குற்றமே கூறி விடும்.
transliteration:
Atram maraikkum perumai sirumaidhaan
kutrame koori vidum.
current_meaning: Greatness covers up the weaknesses of others; littleness speaks of nothing but their faults.
elementary_explanation: If a friend trips and falls in the playground, a kind person helps them up and doesn't laugh. A mean person runs around telling everyone, 'Did you see him fall?' Valluvar says greatness is the helping hand, and smallness is the tattletale.
university_explanation: Atram (அற்றம்) means a weak, exposed or shameful point, literally a gap or defenceless state; maraikkum (மறைக்கும்) is 'conceals'. Against this, sirumai kutrame kooRi vidum (குற்றமே கூறி விடும்): 'littleness will speak out only faults', the emphatic -e (ஏ) on kutram marking that it says nothing else. Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah expand the contrast: the great speak of others' merits and hide their failings, the small hide their merits and broadcast their failings. Pope's 'Greatness will hide a neighbour's shame; / Meanness his faults to all the world proclaim' follows this reading. The chapter thus ends on how the great treat others, after nine couplets on how they hold themselves. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கடன்என்ப நல்லவை எல்லாம் கடன்அறிந்து
சான்றாண்மை மேற்கொள் பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Kadanenpa nallavai ellaam kadanarindhu
saandraanmai merkol pavarkku.
current_meaning: For those who know what is due from them and take up the life of perfected character, every good thing is said to be simply their duty, something they do as a matter of course.
elementary_explanation: Some children help clear the table only when someone asks and then want a sticker for it. Others just do it every day because that is who they are. Valluvar says truly good people are like the second kind: being kind and helpful is not an extra for them, it is just their everyday job.
university_explanation: The chapter title saandraanmai (சான்றாண்மை, from saandror, 'the full, the accomplished', and aanmai, 'mastery, the bearing of a quality') names the fullness of noble character; the related noun saalbu (சால்பு, 'abundance, completeness') recurs throughout the chapter. The opening couplet turns on kadan (கடன், 'debt, duty'): for one who knows his kadan and undertakes (merkol, மேற்கொள்) saandraanmai, all good things (nallavai ellaam) are themselves called duty. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses that for such a person all good things become 'natural duty' (இயல்பான கடமை), and Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan both render it as good qualities becoming one's very nature, the line of interpretation that follows the traditional commentary of Parimelazhagar, in which virtue is no longer a burden chosen case by case but an obligation already accepted. Pope's 'All goodly things are duties to the men, they say' keeps the reported-speech force of enpa (என்ப, 'they say'), marking this as received wisdom. Sivayogi Sivakumar on ytamizh reverses the predicate ('the obligatory duty is the good things'), a minor variation in emphasis rather than in sense. The chapter follows Perumai (Greatness, ch. 98) in the Kudiyiyal and is followed by Panbudaimai (Courtesy, ch. 100). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
குணநலம் சான்றோர் நலனே பிறநலம்
எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று.
transliteration:
Kunanalam saandror nalane piranalam
ennalaththu ulladhooum andru.
current_meaning: The real excellence of the noble is the excellence of their character; every other kind of excellence does not count among true goods at all.
elementary_explanation: A shiny new bike, a nice haircut or a fancy pair of shoes can look great. But Valluvar says the thing that really makes a person beautiful is a kind and honest heart. Everything else is just wrapping paper.
university_explanation: The couplet sets kunanalam (குணநலம், 'the goodness of qualities, beauty of character') against piranalam (பிறநலம், 'other goods'). The noble (saandror) have only one nalam (நலம், 'good, beauty, excellence') worth the name; the other kinds are not counted 'among any good' (ennalaththu ulladhooum andru, எந்நலத்து உள்ளதூஉம் அன்று), where ulladhooum shows the alapedai (vowel lengthening) that fills out the metre. Solomon Pappaiah and Mu. Karunanidhi read nalam as beauty (அழகு), contrasting inner beauty of character with outward beauty of form, while Mu. Varadarasanar keeps the more general 'good'; Pope's prose rendering, following the older commentarial tradition associated with Parimelazhagar, understands the other goods as sensual delights. Both readings make the same claim: for the perfected person only character counts. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அன்புநாண் ஒப்புரவு கண்ணோட்டம் வாய்மையொடு
ஐந்துசால் ஊன்றிய தூண்.
transliteration:
Anbunaan oppuravu kannottam vaaimaiyodu
aindhusaal oondriya thoon.
current_meaning: Love, a sense of shame at wrongdoing, generosity to all, kindly regard for others and truthfulness are the five pillars on which perfect character rests.
elementary_explanation: Think of a tree house held up by five strong posts. If one post breaks, the house wobbles. Valluvar says a good person is held up by five posts too: loving others, feeling shy about doing wrong, sharing, being kind, and telling the truth.
university_explanation: This is the chapter's architectural image: saalbu (perfection) is a load resting on five pillars (aindhu ... oondriya thoon, ஐந்து ... ஊன்றிய தூண்). The five are anbu (அன்பு, 'affection'), naan (நாண், 'shame', specifically recoil from blameworthy deeds, as Pappaiah glosses பழி பாவங்களுக்கு நாணுதல்), oppuravu (ஒப்புரவு, 'benevolence to all, sharing what one has gathered', the subject of ch. 22), kannottam (கண்ணோட்டம், 'kindly regard', literally 'running of the eye', the subject of ch. 58) and vaaimai (வாய்மை, 'truthfulness', ch. 30). Commentators differ on how to parse saal: most take ஐந்து சால்பு ஊன்றிய தூண் as 'the five pillars that bear saalbu', while Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as pillars of the 'vessel' of perfection; Pope renders 'pillars five of perfect virtue's resting-place'. Karunanidhi glosses oppuravu as 'honouring the world's conduct' and kannottam as 'compassionate acts', showing how the virtues shade into each other. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கொல்லா நலத்தது நோன்மை பிறர்தீமை
சொல்லா நலத்தது சால்பு.
transliteration:
Kollaa nalaththadhu nonmai pirardheemai
sollaa nalaththadhu saalbu.
current_meaning: Austerity rests on the goodness of not killing; perfection rests on the goodness of not speaking of other people's faults.
elementary_explanation: A good person does not hurt any living creature, not even a bug. And a really good person also does not go around telling everyone the bad things someone else did. Valluvar says the first is the heart of being holy, and the second is the heart of being truly good.
university_explanation: A balanced couplet built on two parallel phrases: kollaa nalam (கொல்லா நலம், 'the goodness of not killing') grounds nonmai (நோன்மை, 'austerity, penance', glossed as தவம் by Varadarasanar and Kesikan), while sollaa nalam (சொல்லா நலம், 'the goodness of not telling') grounds saalbu. Pirar theemai (பிறர்தீமை) may mean either others' faults or the wrongs others have done; Karunanidhi takes the second ('not pointing out the harm others do'), the majority the first. The pairing ties this chapter to Kollaamai (ch. 33) and Purangooraamai (Not Backbiting, ch. 19), and suggests that just as non-killing is the essence of the ascetic, refusal to broadcast faults is the essence of the noble householder. Pope's 'penitence' for nonmai is archaic; 'austerity' is closer. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads nonmai more broadly as 'sustaining life without destroying'. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல் பணிதல் அதுசான்றோர்
மாற்றாரை மாற்றும் படை.
transliteration:
Aatruvaar aatral panidhal adhusaandror
maatraarai maatrum padai.
current_meaning: The real strength of the capable is humility; it is the weapon with which the noble turn their enemies from enmity.
elementary_explanation: When someone is cross with you, shouting back usually makes it worse. But if you speak gently and say sorry, the angry person often calms down and even becomes your friend. Valluvar says being humble is the strongest tool a good person has.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on the root aatru (ஆற்று, 'to accomplish, to be able'): aatruvaar aatral (ஆற்றுவார் ஆற்றல்), 'the power of those who can achieve', is panidhal (பணிதல், 'bending, humility'). In the second line maatraar (மாற்றார், 'adversaries') are 'changed' (maatrum, மாற்றும்) by this padai (படை, 'weapon, army'), a deliberate pun. Most modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Karunanidhi) read the second line as humility turning enemies away from enmity; Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan, nearer the older commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, read the first line more concretely as the achiever's skill in winning over helpers by bowing to them. Pope's 'Submission is the might of men of mighty acts; the sage / With that same weapon stills his foeman's rage' captures both senses. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சால்பிற்குக் கட்டளை யாதெனின் தோல்வி
துலையல்லார் கண்ணும் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Saalbirkuk kattalai yaadhenin tholvi
thulaiyallaar kannum kolal.
current_meaning: If you ask what the touchstone of perfection is, it is the willingness to accept defeat even at the hands of those who are not one's equals.
elementary_explanation: It is easy to say 'You win' to a big champion. It is much harder to say it to a younger child who beat you at a game. Valluvar says being able to lose gracefully, even to someone smaller, is the real test of a good person.
university_explanation: Kattalai (கட்டளை) here is the touchstone (உரைகல்) used to test gold, as Varadarasanar and Pappaiah gloss it: saalbu is gold, and its test is tholvi ... kolal (தோல்வி ... கொளல், 'accepting defeat'). Thulai allaar (துலையல்லார்), literally 'those not of the same balance (thulai, துலை)', are one's inferiors; the particle -um in kannum (கண்ணும், 'even with') makes the point that yielding to a superior is no test at all. Kesikan spells out the contrast: the defeat one would accept from one's betters must be accepted even from lesser people. Pope's verse ('What is perfection's test? The equal mind. / To bear repulse from even meaner men resigned') introduces 'equal mind' as a gloss rather than a translation. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads thulaiyallaar as those 'unfit to accept defeat', a less common construal. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்னாசெய் தார்க்கும் இனியவே செய்யாக்கால்
என்ன பயத்ததோ சால்பு.
transliteration:
Innaasey thaarkkum iniyave seyyaakkaal
enna payaththadho saalbu.
current_meaning: What use is perfect character if it does not do kind things even to those who have done one harm?
elementary_explanation: Being nice to people who are nice to you is easy. Valluvar asks a harder question: what if someone was mean to you? He says that being kind back to them is what really shows you are a good person.
university_explanation: The couplet is a rhetorical question: if one does not do iniyavai (இனியவை, 'pleasant, kind things') even to those who did innaa (இன்னா, 'painful, harmful things'), of what use (enna payaththadho, என்ன பயத்ததோ) is saalbu? The -um of thaarkkum (தார்க்கும், 'even to those who did') carries the force. It restates for the noble householder the teaching of Innaa Seyyaamai (ch. 32), especially Kural 314 (inna seydhaarai oruththal avar naana nannayam seydhu vidal), and all modern commentators (Varadarasanar, Pappaiah, Karunanidhi, Kesikan) agree on the plain sense. Note that the English section for this couplet on ytamizh.com is misaligned: its 'Couplet Explanation' belongs to Kural 946 on overeating and the line printed as the couplet is Pope's prose explanation, so it should not be relied on here. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்மை ஒருவற்கு இளிவன்று சால்பென்னும்
திண்மைஉண் டாகப் பெறின்.
transliteration:
Inmai oruvarku ilivandru saalbennum
thinmaiun daakap perin.
current_meaning: Poverty is no disgrace to a person who possesses the inner strength called perfection of character.
elementary_explanation: Some people have lots of toys and money, and some have very little. Valluvar says having little is nothing to be ashamed of, as long as you are honest, kind and strong inside. That inner strength is worth more than any treasure.
university_explanation: Inmai (இன்மை, 'having nothing, poverty') is not ilivu (இளிவு, 'disgrace') for one who has gained the thinmai (திண்மை, 'firmness, solidity') called saalbu. The image of perfection as a kind of solidity anticipates the stability of Kural 989. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Karunanidhi all read inmai as material poverty, and Karunanidhi adds that such a person treats saalbu itself as wealth; Sivayogi Sivakumar widens inmai to 'hardships'. Textual note: ytamizh.com reads இளிவன்று (ilivandru, 'is not disgrace'), the standard reading supported by the commentaries' gloss இழிவு; thirukkural.net's main text prints இனிவன்று, which appears to be a typographical error (ன for ள), since its own commentaries gloss the word as இழிவு. This edition follows இளிவன்று. Placed just before the chapters on Nalkuravu (Poverty, ch. 105) and Iravu (Begging, ch. 106), the couplet establishes that character, not wealth, sets the limits of dignity.

tamil:
ஊழி பெயரினும் தாம்பெயரார் சான்றாண்மைக்கு
ஆழி எனப்படு வார்.
transliteration:
Oozhi peyarinum thaampeyaraar saandraanmaikku
aazhi enappadu vaar.
current_meaning: Those who are called the ocean of perfect character will not change, even if the ages themselves change.
elementary_explanation: A big rock on the beach stays in the same place year after year while the waves, the weather and the people all change around it. Valluvar says truly good people are like that: whatever happens around them, they stay good.
university_explanation: Oozhi (ஊழி) is the cosmic age or aeon, and its 'shifting' (peyarinum, பெயரினும், 'even if it moves') evokes the dissolution at the end of an age, when, in Indian cosmology, the seas break their bounds. Against this, those called aazhi (ஆழி) of saandraanmai do not shift (thaam peyaraar, தாம்பெயரார்). Aazhi can mean either 'ocean' or 'shore, boundary', and the commentators divide: Varadarasanar and Karunanidhi take it as ocean ('the ocean of perfection'), while Pappaiah and Kesikan, with Pope ('of perfect virtue's sea the shore'), read it as the shore that holds the sea in, an image which sharpens the contrast, since the shore holds even when the seas of the age-end overflow. Pope's line 'Who, though the fates should fail' renders oozhi loosely as fate. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads oozhi as ordinary change over time. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சான்றவர் சான்றாண்மை குன்றின் இருநிலந்தான்
தாங்காது மன்னோ பொறை.
transliteration:
Saandravar saandraanmai kundrin irunilandhaan
thaangaadhu manno porai.
current_meaning: If the noble were to fall short in their nobility, even this great earth could not bear its burden.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a big table held up by a few strong legs. If those legs get weak, everything on the table comes crashing down. Valluvar says good people are like those legs for the whole world: if they stop being good, the world cannot hold itself up.
university_explanation: The closing couplet extends saandraanmai from personal virtue to cosmic support. If the saandravar (சான்றவர், 'the perfected') should decline (kundrin, குன்றின்) in their saandraanmai, the 'great earth' (irunilam, இருநிலம்) itself could not bear (thaangaadhu, தாங்காது) its porai (பொறை, 'burden'); manno (மன்னோ) is an emphatic particle. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kesikan read porai as the earth's burden, so that the noble become, with the five pillars of Kural 983, the hidden supports of the world; Karunanidhi instead takes porai as 'patience', reading that the world would not patiently tolerate such a decline. Sivayogi Sivakumar's reading of irunilam as the 'two states' of inner and outer life is idiosyncratic. Pope: 'The mighty earth its burthen to sustain must cease, / If perfect virtue of the perfect men decrease.' The idea that the righteous sustain the world appears in many traditions, and here completes the chapter's arc from personal duty (981) to the stability of the world. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
எண்பதத்தால் எய்தல் எளிதென்ப யார்மாட்டும்
பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு.
transliteration:
Enpadhaththaal eydhal elidhenpa yaarmaattum
panputaimai ennum vazhakku.
current_meaning: People say that for someone who is easy for anyone to approach, the noble way called courtesy comes easily.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a class helper whose door is always open, who smiles at every kid, big or small, and listens. Being kind and polite is easy for that helper because they already let everyone come close. Valluvar says good manners grow out of being easy to reach.
university_explanation: The chapter on panbudaimai (பண்புடைமை, 'possession of refined character, courtesy') opens with a practical claim: the path is easy for the one who has en-padham (எண்பதம்), 'easy access', the quality of being approachable (எளிய செவ்வி) to everyone, yaar-maattum (யார்மாட்டும், 'towards whomsoever'). Puliyur Kesikan on thirukkural.net and Mu. Varadarasanar on ytamizh both gloss en-padham as எளிய செவ்வி, availability to all comers, and vazhakku (வழக்கு) as the established good path or usage; Solomon Pappaiah adds that the claim is reported, 'say the learned' (நூலோர் கூறுவர்), reflecting the verb enpa (என்ப, 'they say'). Sivayogi Sivakumar's reading of en as 'numbers' (speaking in words as plain as numerals) is an idiosyncratic minority interpretation not shared by the classical glosses. Pope renders the couplet 'Who easy access give to every man, they say, / Of kindly courtesy will learn with ease the way', and the same accessibility motif appears in the earlier kural 386 on the king who is kaatchikku eliyan (easy of audience). Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Saanraanmai (ch. 99), the chapter turns from the inner perfection of the noble to its outward social face. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அன்புடைமை ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல் இவ்விரண்டும்
பண்புடைமை என்னும் வழக்கு.
transliteration:
Anputaimai aandra kutippiraththal ivvirantum
panputaimai ennum vazhakku.
current_meaning: Loving kindness toward others and birth into a worthy family: these two together make up the way called courtesy.
elementary_explanation: Think of a kind heart as the seed and a good home as the garden it grows in. When a child has both a loving heart and a family that teaches good ways, gentle manners bloom. Valluvar says courtesy needs both.
university_explanation: The second couplet names the two roots of panbudaimai: anbudaimai (அன்புடைமை, 'possession of love', the title of chapter 8) and aandra kudip-piraththal (ஆன்ற குடிப்பிறத்தல், 'being born in an eminent, accomplished family'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar take aandra kudi as a high or noble family, while Solomon Pappaiah reinterprets it as a family that 'lives in harmony with the world' (உலகத்தோடு ஒத்து வாழும் குடும்பம்), softening the hereditary emphasis; Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as living a birth worth reflecting on. Pope's 'Benevolence and high born dignity, / These two are beaten paths of courtesy' preserves vazhakku (வழக்கு) as a 'beaten path' or established usage. The kural links this chapter back to Kudimai (ch. 96, 'Nobility of family'), which places good family upbringing at the base of character; modern readers often stress that the second element is about formation and tradition rather than caste rank. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உறுப்பொத்தல் மக்களொப்பு அன்றால் வெறுத்தக்க
பண்பொத்தல் ஒப்பதாம் ஒப்பு.
transliteration:
Uruppoththal makkaloppu andraal veruththakka
panpoththal oppadhaam oppu.
current_meaning: Having the same body parts does not make people truly alike; real likeness is likeness in the good, agreeable qualities of character.
elementary_explanation: Two dolls can look exactly the same on the outside, but one might be stuffed with cotton and the other with sharp pins. People are like that too: having two eyes and two hands like someone does not make you like them. Being kind like them does.
university_explanation: Uruppu-oththal (உறுப்பொத்தல், 'sameness of limbs') is denied the status of makkal-oppu (மக்களொப்பு, 'likeness among humans'); true oppu is panb-oththal (பண்பொத்தல்), likeness in qualities. The crux is veruththakka (வெறுத்தக்க): Mu. Varadarasanar glosses it as 'fit to be joined' (பொருந்தத்தக்க), Solomon Pappaiah as qualities that unite heart with heart, and Pope as 'kindred quality' ('Similitude of kindred quality makes likeness true'), reflecting the older commentarial reading of வெறு as 'to be close, to cohere'. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads it in the modern sense 'hateful', yielding 'likeness in shunning what deserves shunning', a minority interpretation. Kalaignar draws the strong conclusion that only those alike in good qualities deserve to be counted as human at all, which anticipates kural 997. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நயனொடு நன்றி புரிந்த பயனுடையார்
பண்புபா ராட்டும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Nayanotu nandri purindha payanutaiyaar
panpupaa raattum ulaku.
current_meaning: The world praises the character of those who are useful to others because they love justice and do good.
elementary_explanation: When a kid is fair in games and also helps others when they fall, everyone on the playground says, 'She's so nice!' Valluvar says people love and praise those who are both fair and helpful.
university_explanation: The couplet pairs nayan (நயன், 'justice, equity, fairness') with nanri (நன்றி, 'beneficence, doing good'), and calls those who 'cherish' (purindha, புரிந்த) both payan-udaiyaar (பயனுடையார்), people who are of real use to others. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses the pair as நீதியும் நன்மையும், Pappaiah as நீதியும் அறமும், and Pope's prose 'equity and charity' follows the same traditional line. The result is that ulagu (உலகு, 'the world', i.e. the discerning public) 'praises' (paaraattum, பாராட்டும்) their panbu. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes nayan as conduct that gives delight, a looser reading. The kural shows that courtesy in Valluvar is not mere politeness of speech but includes just and beneficial action. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நகையுள்ளும் இன்னா திகழ்ச்சி பகையுள்ளும்
பண்புள பாடறிவார் மாட்டு.
transliteration:
Nakaiyullum innaa thikazhchchi pakaiyullum
panpula paadarivaar maattu.
current_meaning: Mocking someone hurts even when it is only a joke; so those who understand people keep their courtesy even toward enemies.
elementary_explanation: Calling someone a silly name 'just for fun' can still make them cry inside. Kids who really understand feelings don't do it, not even to a kid they're cross with. Valluvar says being polite even to someone you don't like is a sign of real wisdom.
university_explanation: The first line states a psychological fact: igazhchi (இகழ்ச்சி, 'contempt, ridicule') is innaa (இன்னா, 'painful') even within nagai (நகை, 'laughter, jest'). The second draws the ethical conclusion: among paadarivaar (பாடறிவார், 'those who know the nature or proper manner', from பாடு, 'way, condition'), panbu remains even within pagai (பகை, 'enmity'). Mu. Varadarasanar reads the paadarivaar as those who act knowing others' nature; Pappaiah expands that such people do not ridicule even foes; Pope renders 'Contempt is evil though in sport. They who man's nature know, / E'en in their wrath, a courteous mind will show.' The jingle nagaiyullum ... pagaiyullum binds jest and enmity as the two tests of courtesy. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பண்புடையார்ப் பட்டுண்டு உலகம் அதுஇன்றேல்
மண்புக்கு மாய்வது மன்.
transliteration:
Panputaiyaarp pattuntu ulakam adhuindrel
manpukku maaivadhu man.
current_meaning: The world keeps going because it rests on people of courteous character; without them it would sink into the earth and perish.
elementary_explanation: A tent stands up because of its poles. Take the poles away and the whole tent falls flat on the ground. Valluvar says kind, well-mannered people are the poles that hold up the whole world.
university_explanation: Ulagam (உலகம்) here means the ongoing life of human society; it 'exists' (undu, உண்டு) because it is pattu (பட்டு, 'resting upon, attached to') the panbudaiyaar (பண்புடையார், 'people of character'). Without that support it would man-pukku maaivadhu (மண்புக்கு மாய்வது), 'enter the earth and perish', the final man (மன்) being an emphatic particle. Mu. Varadarasanar glosses pattu as 'by being joined to' the courteous; Kalaignar reads ulagam as 'the conduct of the world'; Pope's prose 'The (way of the) world subsists by contact with the good' follows the traditional line. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes the second line very differently, as 'even supplication would be meaningless', which departs from the classical gloss of man-pukku as 'entering the soil'. The kural echoes kural 571 on kannottam, where the world exists through the gracious. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அரம்போலும் கூர்மைய ரேனும் மரம்போல்வர்
மக்கட்பண்பு இல்லா தவர்.
transliteration:
Arampolum koormaiya renum marampolvar
makkatpanpu illaa thavar.
current_meaning: Those without humane qualities are no better than trees, even if their minds are as sharp as a file.
elementary_explanation: A pencil sharpener is very sharp, but it can't give you a hug or say sorry. Valluvar says a person can be super clever, but if they aren't kind they are like a tree trunk: standing there, but not really acting like a person.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on the rhyme aram (அரம், 'file, rasp') and maram (மரம், 'tree'): those who lack makkat-panbu (மக்கட்பண்பு, 'the quality proper to human beings') are 'like trees' even if they have a file's koormai (கூர்மை, 'sharpness'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Pappaiah both gloss maram as ஓரறிவுயிர், 'a one-sensed being', invoking the classical Tamil (and Jain) grading of living beings by the number of their senses, so the insult is precise: an intellect without humanity sinks to the lowest rung of life. Pope renders 'Though sharp their wit as file, as blocks they must remain, / Whose souls are void of courtesy humane'. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads aram as a sharp cutting tool and makkat-panbu as 'humanitarianism'. The kural extends the argument of 993 from likeness to humanity itself. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நண்பாற்றார் ஆகி நயமில செய்வார்க்கும்
பண்பாற்றார் ஆதல் கடை.
transliteration:
Nanpaatraar aaki nayamila seyvaarkkum
panpaatraar aadhal katai.
current_meaning: Failing to be courteous, even toward those who are unfriendly and do us wrong, is the lowest disgrace.
elementary_explanation: If a classmate keeps being mean to you, it is tempting to be mean back. But Valluvar says the really strong thing is to stay polite anyway. Being rude back would make you lose something precious of your own.
university_explanation: The couplet carries the chapter's ethic to its hardest case. Nanb-aatraar (நண்பாற்றார்) are those who 'do not practise friendship', and nayam-ila seyvaar (நயமில செய்வார்) those who 'do unpleasant, unjust things'; even toward them, to be panb-aatraar (பண்பாற்றார், 'not practising courtesy') is kadai (கடை), 'the lowest, the worst'. Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it as a disgrace (இழிவு) to abandon courtesy in the face of hostility; Kalaignar adds patience (பொறுமை) as the means. Pope's 'Though men with all unfriendly acts and wrongs assail, / 'Tis uttermost disgrace in courtesy to fail' captures the parallel of nanbaatraar ... panbaatraar. The kural echoes kural 314 on 'shaming' wrongdoers by doing them good. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்க்கு மாயிரு ஞாலம்
பகலும்பாற் பட்டன்று இருள்.
transliteration:
Nakalvallar allaarkku maayiru gnaalam
pakalumpaar pattandru irul.
current_meaning: For those who cannot share in friendly, cheerful company, this vast wide world lies in darkness even in broad daylight.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a sunny day at the park, but you won't play, laugh, or talk with anyone. Even with the sun shining, it would feel gloomy. Valluvar says a heart that can't smile and join in makes the whole world feel dark.
university_explanation: Nagal vallar allaar (நகல்வல்லர் அல்லார்) are 'those not able to laugh', that is, unable to mix with others and share friendly cheer; for them maa-iru gnaalam (மாயிரு ஞாலம், 'the great, vast earth') is, even by day (pagalum), fallen into darkness (paal patta-andru irul, பாற்பட்டன்று இருள்). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses nagal as 'mingling with others and rejoicing' (பிறரோடு கலந்து பழகி மகிழ), Pappaiah ties it explicitly to lack of good character, and Kalaignar to inability to enjoy friends; Pope's prose 'To those who cannot rejoice, the wide world is buried darkness even in (broad) day light' follows this line. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads nagal as 'harmonizing with others' and iru as 'two-fold', an idiosyncratic segmentation. The transliteration of gnaalam varies across sites (Gnaalam on ytamizh, ñālam on thirukkural.net). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பண்பிலான் பெற்ற பெருஞ்செல்வம் நன்பால்
கலந்தீமை யால்திரிந் தற்று.
transliteration:
Panpilaan petra perunjelvam nanpaal
kalandheemai yaaldhirin thatru.
current_meaning: Great wealth that comes to a person without courtesy is like good milk spoiled by an unclean vessel.
elementary_explanation: Pour fresh milk into a dirty cup and it turns sour and yucky. Valluvar says money is like that milk: if it goes to a rude, unkind person, it turns sour and does nobody any good.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with a domestic simile: the perum-selvam (பெருஞ்செல்வம், 'great wealth') of the panbilaan (பண்பிலான், 'man without courtesy') is like nan-paal (நன்பால், 'good milk') that has 'turned' (thirindhu, திரிந்து) through kalam-theemai (கலந்தீமை, 'defect of the vessel'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read kalan as the container (கலம், பாத்திரம்), Kalaignar specifying a vessel coated with verdigris (களிம்பு); Pope's verse 'Like sweet milk soured because in filthy vessel poured' agrees, while his prose 'will perish like pure milk spoilt by the impurity of the vessel' stresses waste. The segmentation kalan + theemai, rather than kalandhu + theemai ('mixed with evil'), is the standard one; Sivayogi Sivakumar's 'by the evil mixed with it' reflects the alternative split. The kural also bridges to the next chapter, Nanriyil Selvam (ch. 101, 'Useless wealth'). Transliterations differ slightly (yaaldhirinh thatru on ytamizh; yaaldhirin thatru on thirukkural.net), but the Tamil text is identical on both sites.

tamil:
வைத்தான்வாய் சான்ற பெரும்பொருள் அஃதுண்ணான்
செத்தான் செயக்கிடந்தது இல்.
transliteration:
Vaiththaanvaai Saandra Perumporul Aqdhunnaan
Seththaan Seyakkitandhadhu Il
current_meaning: A man who fills his house with vast wealth and never enjoys it is as good as dead, for there is nothing that wealth has done through him.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a boy who fills his whole room with sweets but never eats one and never shares one. The sweets just sit there until they go stale. Valluvar says a person who piles up money like that and never uses it might as well not be there at all.
university_explanation: The chapter title நன்றியில் செல்வம் uses நன்றி in its older sense of 'benefit, good' rather than 'gratitude': this is wealth that does no good to anyone. In vaittaan-vaay (வைத்தான்வாய்) வாய் means 'place', so the wealth 'fills the place where he stored it'; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses இடமெல்லாம் நிறைந்த, and Puliyur Kesikan (thirukkural.net) adds that the man does not eat it 'through avarice' (உலோபத்தால்). The second line is elliptical: seththaan (செத்தான்) can be read either as 'he is (equivalent to) a dead man', as Solomon Pappaiah and Pope take it ('Is dead'), or as 'when he dies, there is nothing left done (by the wealth)', as Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar render it; both readings yield the same verdict that unused wealth achieves nothing. The chapter stands in the Kudiyiyal after Panbudaimai (ch. 100), turning from courtesy to the social uselessness of hoarded riches, and complements the earlier chapters on Ithal (ch. 23) and Oppuravu (ch. 22). The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பொருளானாம் எல்லாமென்று ஈயாது இவறும்
மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Porulaanaam Ellaamendru Eeyaadhu Ivarum
Marulaanaam Maanaap Pirappu
current_meaning: Thinking that wealth can do everything, a man clings to it and gives nothing away; that very delusion leads him to a debased birth.
elementary_explanation: Some people think, 'If I just have enough money, I'll have everything!' So they grip their money tight and never share. Valluvar says this is a big mistake, like a confused traveller holding the wrong map, and it leads them to a very sad place.
university_explanation: The first line reports the miser's creed, poruLaal aam ellaam ('by wealth everything is achieved'), and his conduct, eeyaadhu ivaRum ('not giving, he clings'); ivaRu- denotes tight-fisted holding, the same root as இவறல் (miserliness) condemned among royal faults in Kural 432. The second line names the result: maruL (மருள், 'delusion, bewilderment') produces maaNaap piRappu, 'an un-excellent birth'. Mu. Varadarasanar keeps this general ('a birth without distinction'), Kalaignar reads it this-worldly ('a base creature'), while Solomon Pappaiah and Pope's explanation ('will be born a demon') follow the classical line that specifies a ghost or demon birth (பேய்ப் பிறப்பு); Sivayogi Sivakumar reads it as an endless, graceless cycle of births. The phrase மருளானாம் மாணாப் பிறப்பு also closes Kural 351, where delusion about what is real is said to cause such a birth, so Valluvar here treats the miser's faith in money as a species of metaphysical error. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஈட்டம் இவறி இசைவேண்டா ஆடவர்
தோற்றம் நிலக்குப் பொறை.
transliteration:
Eettam Ivari Isaiventaa Aatavar
Thotram Nilakkup Porai
current_meaning: Men who are greedy only for piling up wealth and care nothing for an honourable name are, by their very existence, a burden to the earth.
elementary_explanation: Think of a squirrel that hides a thousand nuts and never lets another animal have one, and no one in the forest has a kind word for it. Valluvar says people who only collect and collect, and never do anything good that others would remember, are just heavy weight on the ground.
university_explanation: The couplet sets two objects of desire against each other: eettam (ஈட்டம், 'accumulation', from ஈட்டு- 'to earn, amass') and isai (இசை, 'fame, renown'), which in the Kural is earned chiefly by giving (compare Pugazh, ch. 24, beginning 'ஈதல் இசைபட வாழ்தல்'). Those who 'cling to accumulation and do not want renown' have a thoatram (தோற்றம், 'appearance, birth, existence') that is poRai (பொறை, 'burden, weight') to the earth; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar read தோற்றம் as 'being born and living', Pope as appearing 'on the stage of being'. Solomon Pappaiah adds a competitive nuance: they want to amass more than others. Sivayogi Sivakumar reads இசை as 'interest/inclination' (இசைவு) beyond acquiring wealth, a minority interpretation. The 'burden of the earth' image echoes Kural 239, where the land bearing a body without fame loses its yield. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
எச்சமென்று என்எண்ணுங் கொல்லோ ஒருவரால்
நச்சப் படாஅ தவன்.
transliteration:
Echchamendru Enennung Kollo Oruvaraal
Nachchap Pataaa Thavan
current_meaning: What can a man whom no one loves expect to leave behind him as his legacy?
elementary_explanation: When a kind teacher retires, the children remember her stories and her hugs for years. But if someone never helped anyone, what will people remember about him when he is gone? Valluvar asks: what is left of a person nobody loved?
university_explanation: The key word is echcham (எச்சம், 'remainder, what is left over'), which in the Kural can mean posterity or a lasting name; Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar gloss 'what remains after his death', Solomon Pappaiah 'what will stand to recall him after his time'. The man is described as oruvaraal nachchap padaaa-thavan, 'one not desired by even a single person'; nachchu (நச்சு, 'to desire, love') returns in Kural 1008, where the same unloved man's wealth is a poisonous tree, so the chapter plays on நச்சு 'love' and நச்சு 'poison'. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the reason for his unpopularity, that he helped no one. Pope's explanation narrows echcham to what the miser can count as his own 'in the world to come', a reading that follows the classical tendency to interpret legacy in terms of merit for the next life. The rhetorical question (என் எண்ணும் கொல்லோ, 'what, pray, does he think?') turns the couplet into a mock of the miser's planning. The text is identical on both sources (ytamizh prints எண்ணுங் with the same ங்).

tamil:
கொடுப்பதூஉம் துய்ப்பதூஉம் இல்லார்க்கு அடுக்கிய
கோடியுண் டாயினும் இல்.
transliteration:
Kotuppadhooum Thuyppadhooum Illaarkku Atukkiya
Kotiyun Taayinum Il
current_meaning: For those who neither give nor enjoy, wealth amounts to nothing, even if they possess crores heaped upon crores.
elementary_explanation: If you have a big box of crayons but never draw with them and never lend them to a friend, it is just like having no crayons at all. Valluvar says money works the same way: if you never use it and never share it, you are really poor.
university_explanation: The couplet names the two proper uses of wealth, koduppadhu (கொடுப்பது, 'giving') and thuyppadhu (துய்ப்பது, 'enjoying, consuming'), with the emphatic lengthening -ūum (கொடுப்பதூஉம், துய்ப்பதூஉம்) marking each as indispensable. Adukkiya kodi (அடுக்கிய கோடி) means 'crores stacked one upon another'; Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'many crores ever increasing'. The verdict il (இல், 'there is not') says such people are effectively without wealth; Pope renders the sense as 'they are poor'. Solomon Pappaiah adds the qualifier that giving should be to those in need and enjoying should be as need requires, guarding against reading the couplet as licence for extravagance. The two-fold scheme parallels the Sanskrit gnomic triad of dāna, bhoga and nāśa (giving, enjoyment, destruction) found in Bhartrihari. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஏதம் பெருஞ்செல்வம் தான்துவ்வான் தக்கார்க்கொன்று
ஈதல் இயல்பிலா தான்.
transliteration:
Edham Perunjelvam Thaandhuvvaan Thakkaarkkondru
Eedhal Iyalpilaa Thaan
current_meaning: One who neither enjoys his great wealth himself nor has it in his nature to give something to the worthy is a blight upon that wealth.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a lovely garden where the owner never sits and never lets anyone else pick a flower. The garden is wasted, and the owner is like a sickness that keeps it from doing any good. Valluvar says a stingy rich person is like that sickness for his own money.
university_explanation: The opening word edham (ஏதம், 'harm, fault, affliction, disease') is the predicate, and its subject is the man described in the rest of the couplet: thaan thuvvaan (தான் துவ்வான், 'he himself does not enjoy') and thakkaarkku ondru eedhal iyalbu ilaan (தக்கார்க்கு ஒன்று ஈதல் இயல்பு இலான், 'one who has no disposition to give even one thing to the worthy'). Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar therefore read him as a disease (நோய்) to his own great wealth, as does Pope's explanation ('a disease to his wealth'); Solomon Pappaiah inverts it, making the wealth a disease in his keeping, and Sivayogi Sivakumar reads that he does harm to himself. The word iyalbu (இயல்பு, 'nature') stresses that the fault is temperamental, not circumstantial, and thakkaar (தக்கார், 'the deserving') narrows the duty of giving to worthy recipients, a classical criterion of proper gifts. Pope's verse rendering ('misery to men of churlish heart') follows the alternative sense. The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
அற்றார்க்கொன்று ஆற்றாதான் செல்வம் மிகநலம்
பெற்றாள் தமியள்மூத் தற்று.
transliteration:
Atraarkkondru Aatraadhaan Selvam Mikanalam
Petraal Thamiyalmooth Thatru
current_meaning: The wealth of one who gives nothing to the destitute is like a woman of great beauty who grows old alone, her gifts wasted.
elementary_explanation: Picture the most beautiful flower blooming inside a locked room where nobody ever sees it, until it slowly fades. Valluvar says money that never helps poor people is like that hidden flower: something lovely, wasted.
university_explanation: Atraar (அற்றார், 'those who have nothing, the destitute') are the intended recipients, and aatraadhaan (ஆற்றாதான்) is 'one who does not do (even one thing) for them'. The simile mika nalam petraaL thamiyaL mooththatru (மிக நலம் பெற்றாள் தமியள் மூத்தற்று) compares such wealth to 'a woman endowed with great beauty growing old alone'; Solomon Pappaiah and Pope's explanation specify 'without a husband', Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep 'alone'. The point of the comparison is waste: a good thing that exists to be shared lapses unused, the same logic as the chapter's poisonous-tree image in 1008 and its counterpart in Kural 216, where a generous man's wealth is a fruit tree in the middle of the village. The simile reflects the social world of classical Tamil literature, in which beauty fulfilled in married life is the norm; modern readers may note the period assumption while keeping the moral about unshared resources. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நச்சப் படாதவன் செல்வம் நடுவூருள்
நச்சு மரம்பழுத் தற்று.
transliteration:
Nachchap Pataadhavan Selvam Natuvoorul
Nachchu Marampazhuth Thatru
current_meaning: The wealth of a man whom nobody loves is like a poisonous tree bearing fruit in the middle of the town.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a tree in the middle of the playground covered in shiny fruit, but the fruit is poisonous, so nobody can eat it. Valluvar says a selfish rich person's money is like that tree: right there in front of everyone, but no use to anyone.
university_explanation: The couplet is built on a pun: nachchap padaadhavan (நச்சப் படாதவன், 'one not loved', from நச்சு- 'to desire') and nachchu maram (நச்சு மரம், 'poison tree'). Pope's explanation identifies it as the etty tree (எட்டி, the nux-vomica, Strychnos nux-vomica), and Sivayogi Sivakumar quotes the proverb எட்டி பழுத்தால் என்ன, ஈயாதான் வாழ்ந்தால் என்ன ('what if the etty ripens, what if the non-giver prospers'). The setting naduvooruL (நடுவூருள், 'in the middle of the town') heightens the irony: the fruit is in full view and within reach of all, yet useless. Mu. Varadarasanar supplies the reason the man is unloved, that he helps no one. The image is the exact inverse of Kural 216, where the wealth of the generous is a fruit-bearing tree in the midst of the village, so Valluvar deliberately pairs the two chapters on Oppuravu and Nandriyil Selvam. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அன்பொரீஇத் தற்செற்று அறநோக்காது ஈட்டிய
ஒண்பொருள் கொள்வார் பிறர்.
transliteration:
Anporeeith Tharsetru Aranokkaadhu Eettiya
Onporul Kolvaar Pirar
current_meaning: Shining wealth gathered by abandoning love, denying oneself, and ignoring righteousness will in the end be taken by others.
elementary_explanation: A boy saves all his pocket money, never shares, never buys himself a treat, and even cheats a little to get more. One day he moves away and leaves the jar behind, and other kids spend it. Valluvar says money gathered in such a selfish, unhappy way ends up with someone else.
university_explanation: The couplet lists three things sacrificed in the getting: anbu oreei (அன்பு ஒரீஇ, 'having forsaken love', the -īi lengthening marking the verbal participle), thaR setRu (தற்செற்று, 'having afflicted oneself', i.e. denying oneself comfort), and aRam nokkaadhu (அறம் நோக்காது, 'without regard for virtue'). The resulting oNporuL (ஒண்பொருள், 'bright, glittering wealth') is taken by piRar (பிறர், 'others'). Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Sivayogi Sivakumar read 'others will enjoy it', Kalaignar sharpens it to 'others will plunder it', and Pope's explanation has 'strangers will inherit'; Pope glosses the three omissions as friendship, comfort and charity. Pappaiah reads anbu as love shown to others through giving, which ties the couplet to the chapter's theme rather than to domestic affection. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
சீருடைச் செல்வர் சிறுதுனி மாரி
வறங்கூர்ந் தனையது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Seerutaich Chelvar Sirudhuni Maari
Varangoorn Thanaiyadhu Utaiththu
current_meaning: The brief poverty of generous, honoured rich men is like a rain cloud that has emptied itself for a while; it will soon be full again.
elementary_explanation: A rain cloud pours out all its water on the thirsty fields, and for a little while it looks thin and empty. But soon it fills up again. Valluvar says when kind, generous people run short for a while, it is just like that cloud: they gave a lot, and they will be full again.
university_explanation: After nine couplets on useless wealth, the chapter closes on its positive counterpart. Seerudaich chelvar (சீருடைச் செல்வர்) are 'rich men endowed with excellence', which Mu. Varadarasanar glosses 'famous' and Solomon Pappaiah 'famous for giving to others'. Their siRu thuni (சிறுதுனி) is 'a small distress', read by most commentators as a brief poverty; Pope renders 'brief poverty'. It is compared to maari vaRam koorndhanaiyadhu (மாரி வறங் கூர்ந்தனையது), 'like the rain cloud becoming impoverished', i.e. temporarily spent; Mu. Varadarasanar specifies 'the cloud that can protect the world'. The implication is that the generous man's want is temporary and itself a sign of his giving, as the cloud's emptiness follows its rain. Sivayogi Sivakumar takes a different line, reading the distress as the darkening that precedes rain and turns into good; Kalaignar reads the couplet as saying that even a shadow of poverty on such men is as grave as failed rain. The cloud image recalls Kural 211 on duty that expects no return, like the rain. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கருமத்தால் நாணுதல் நாணுந் திருநுதல்
நல்லவர் நாணுப் பிற.
transliteration:
Karumaththaal naanudhal naanum thirunudhal
nallavar naanup pira.
current_meaning: True shame is shrinking back from a wrong deed; the other kinds of bashfulness are the natural modesty of graceful, bright-browed women.
elementary_explanation: Some kids feel shy when they have to sing in front of the class; that is one kind of shy. But Valluvar says the shame that really matters is the feeling that stops your hand just before you do something mean or wrong. That feeling is like a good friend inside you.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by defining its subject: naanudhal (நாணுதல், 'shrinking, being abashed') that arises karumaththaal (கருமத்தால், 'on account of a deed'), i.e. recoiling from a base act, is the naan (நாண்) of the good. Puliyur Kesikan, following the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, glosses the second line as saying that the other shrinkings of mind, speech and body are the modesty proper to women of good family (thirunudhal nallavar, 'the good ones of beautiful brow'), so Valluvar separates a moral emotion open to everyone from a customary, gendered bashfulness. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, and Pope renders the moral sense as ‘generous shame’. Placed in the Kudiyiyal after Nanriyil Selvam (ch. 101) and before Kudiseyalvagai (ch. 103), the chapter treats naan as the inner guard of the well-born person. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net (ytamizh writes the same words; only spacing differs).

tamil:
ஊணுடை எச்சம் உயிர்க்கெல்லாம் வேறல்ல
நாணுடைமை மாந்தர் சிறப்பு.
transliteration:
Oonudai echcham uyirkkellaam veralla
naanudaimai maandhar sirappu.
current_meaning: Food, clothing and the other necessities are common to every living being; what sets good people apart is a sense of shame.
elementary_explanation: A puppy eats, a bird sleeps, and you eat and sleep too. So what makes a person special? Valluvar says it is the little voice that says “that would be wrong, I'd be ashamed to do it.” Animals don't have that voice. People do.
university_explanation: Oon (ஊண், 'food'), udai (உடை, 'clothing') and echcham (எச்சம், 'the remainder', i.e. the other bodily needs) are veralla (வேறல்ல, 'not different') for all uyir (உயிர், 'living beings'). By contrast naanudaimai (நாணுடைமை, 'the possession of shame') is maandhar sirappu (மாந்தர் சிறப்பு, 'the distinction of humans'). Kesikan and Varadarasanar take the first line to cover all beings and sets of people. Pappaiah narrows the contrast: food and clothing are common to all people, while shame distinguishes the good. Kalaignar explains naanudaimai as avoiding what others condemn. The kural thus makes shame the defining mark of the human, an idea that echoes widely in Indian (Hitopadesha) and Greek (Protagoras) ethics. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஊனைக் குறித்த உயிரெல்லாம் நாண்என்னும்
நன்மை குறித்தது சால்பு.
transliteration:
Oonaik kuriththa uyirellaam naanennum
nanmai kuriththadhu saalpu.
current_meaning: Just as every living being dwells in a body of flesh, perfect nobility dwells in the good quality called shame.
elementary_explanation: A snail lives in its shell and a turtle lives in its shell; they can't live without them. Valluvar says goodness lives inside shame the same way. If you take away a person's shame, their goodness has no home left.
university_explanation: The kural builds an exact parallel. Uyir ellaam oonaik kuriththa (உயிரெல்லாம் ஊனைக் குறித்த): all lives have the body of flesh (ஊன்) as their seat. Saalpu (சால்பு, 'fullness of noble character', the virtue treated in ch. 99, Saanraanmai) has as its seat the nanmai (நன்மை, 'goodness') called naan. The verb kuriththal ('to aim at, to take as one's place') is repeated in both lines. Kesikan presses the image further: as lives never willingly leave their body, saalpu never leaves shame. Kalaignar renders saalpu as maanbu ('dignity'). Pope's ‘perfect virtue ever dwells with shame’ keeps the doubled structure. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அணிஅன்றோ நாணுடைமை சான்றோர்க்கு அஃதின்றேல்
பிணிஅன்றோ பீடு நடை.
transliteration:
Aniandro naanudaimai saandrorkku ahdhindrel
piniandro peedu nadai.
current_meaning: Is not a sense of shame the jewel of the noble? Without it, is not their proud, stately walk a sickness?
