elementary_explanation: Imagine a champion who wins a race and then struts around boasting and laughing at everyone else. It spoils everything, like a sickness. But a champion who wins and stays kind and modest shines like someone wearing a beautiful necklace. Modesty is that necklace.
university_explanation: Two rhetorical questions with ‘andro’ (அன்றோ, ‘is it not?’) frame the kural. Naanudaimai is ani (அணி, 'ornament, jewel') to the saandror (சான்றோர், 'the noble, the perfected'). Without it (ahdhu indrel), their peedu nadai (பீடு நடை, 'gait of eminence, proud bearing') is pini (பிணி, 'disease'). Varadarasanar reads the disease as the proud walk itself. Pappaiah, more pointedly, says it is a disease to those who must watch it. Kalaignar glosses naan here as inward remorse for a wrong done. Pope: ‘without it step of stately pride is piteous thing to see.’ Thirukkural.net prints a final full stop that ytamizh.com omits; the words are otherwise identical, so the difference is only punctuation.

tamil:
பிறர்பழியும் தம்பழியும் நாணுவார் நாணுக்கு
உறைபதி என்னும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Pirarpazhiyum thampazhiyum naanuvaar naanukku
uraipadhi ennum ulagu.
current_meaning: Those who feel ashamed of another's disgrace as much as of their own are the ones the world calls the very home of shame.
elementary_explanation: When your friend gets caught being unkind, do you just laugh? Or do you feel a little hot in the face, as if it were you? Valluvar says the people who feel ashamed even when someone else does wrong are the ones whose hearts are truly good.
university_explanation: Pirar pazhi (பிறர்பழி, 'the blame or disgrace of others') and tham pazhi (தம்பழி, 'one's own disgrace') are set side by side. The one who naanuvaar (நாணுவார், 'feels shame') at both is called by the world naanukku uraipadhi (நாணுக்கு உறைபதி, 'the dwelling-place of shame itself'). Kesikan stresses that such a person weighs the two kinds of blame equally. Pappaiah reads ‘not only one's own but also others' blame’. Pope's couplet, ‘Who feel ashamed for others' guilt as for their own’, follows the same line. The kural extends shame from a private brake to a shared moral sensitivity, which fits the Kudiyiyal's concern with the honour of family and community. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நாண்வேலி கொள்ளாது மன்னோ வியன்ஞாலம்
பேணலர் மேலா யவர்.
transliteration:
Naanveli kollaadhu manno viyangnaalam
paenalar melaa yavar.
current_meaning: The truly great would not want even the whole wide world if it meant giving up the hedge of shame; shame, not the world, is what guards them.
elementary_explanation: A garden has a fence so goats can't come in and eat the flowers. Valluvar says good people keep a fence of shame around their hearts. Even if someone offered them the whole world, they wouldn't trade away that fence.
university_explanation: Naan veli (நாண்வேலி, 'the hedge or fence that is shame') is the central image. The melaayavar (மேலாயவர், 'the superior ones') will not paenal (பேணல், 'cherish, desire') the viyan gnaalam (வியன்ஞாலம், 'vast world') without taking (kollaadhu) that hedge; manno (மன்னோ) is an emphatic particle. Kesikan and Pappaiah, in the line of Parimelazhagar, take it to mean that the great choose shame rather than the wide world as their protection. Varadarasanar reads it as saying the great would not want to live in the wide world without the protecting hedge of shame. Pope gives a more poetic turn: ‘For men of lofty soul the earth's vast realms no charms retain’ unless the hedge stays intact. Sivayogi Sivakumar's modern reading, that one cannot rise to greatness without the hedge, is a minority interpretation. The text is identical on both sites.

tamil:
நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர் உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால்
நாண்துறவார் நாணாள் பவர்.
transliteration:
Naanaal uyiraith thurappar uyirpporuttaal
naanthuravaar naanaal pavar.
current_meaning: Those who live by shame will give up their life for its sake, but will never give up shame to save their life.
elementary_explanation: Some heroes in stories are asked to do something really wrong, like betray a friend, or else they'll be hurt. And they say no, even though it's scary. Valluvar says people with real shame would rather lose everything than do something shameful.
university_explanation: The kural is built as a chiasmus. Naanaal uyiraith thurappar (நாணால் உயிரைத் துறப்பர், 'for shame's sake they renounce life') is mirrored by uyir poruttaal naan thuravaar (உயிர்ப்பொருட்டால் நாண்துறவார், 'for life's sake they do not renounce shame'). Naan aalpavar (நாணாள்பவர், 'those who wield or rule by shame') are its subject. Kesikan frames it as a dilemma: when shame and life cannot both be kept, the noble let life go. Kalaignar substitutes maanam (honour), linking the kural to ch. 97 (Maanam), where similar sentiments appear (e.g. kural 969 on the yak that dies on losing its hair). Pope: ‘The men of modest soul for shame would life an offering make.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பிறர்நாணத் தக்கது தான்நாணா னாயின்
அறம்நாணத் தக்கது உடைத்து.
transliteration:
Pirarnaanath thakkadhu thaannaanaa naayin
aramnaanath thakkadhu udaiththu.
current_meaning: If a person feels no shame at what would make others ashamed, then virtue itself will be ashamed of him and leave.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone does something so rude that everyone watching feels embarrassed, but he just grins. Valluvar says that even Goodness itself would feel embarrassed to be his friend and would quietly walk away from him.
university_explanation: The kural personifies aram (அறம், 'virtue, dharma'). If one does not feel shame (thaan naanaan aayin) at what is pirar naanath thakkadhu (பிறர்நாணத் தக்கது, 'fit to make others ashamed'), then he udaiththu (உடைத்து, 'has in him') something aram naanath thakkadhu, at which virtue itself would blush. There are two lines of interpretation. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar say virtue, ashamed, abandons him. Pappaiah and Kesikan say he harbours a fault at which virtue is ashamed. Kesikan's gloss reads the first line as ‘what onlookers would blame’. Pope's ‘Virtue will shrink away ashamed of thee!’ follows the abandonment reading. The repeated naanath thakkadhu across both lines is characteristic Valluvar wordplay. The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
குலஞ்சுடும் கொள்கை பிழைப்பின் நலஞ்சுடும்
நாணின்மை நின்றக் கடை.
transliteration:
Kulanjudum kolgai pizhaippin nalanjudum
naaninmai nindrak kadai.
current_meaning: A lapse in conduct burns away the good name of one's family; but once shamelessness takes hold, it burns away every good thing a person has.
elementary_explanation: If you break a rule once, people might think less of your family for a while. But if you stop caring at all whether you do wrong, it's like a fire that keeps spreading and burns up everything good about you.
university_explanation: The kural ranks two fires with the same verb, sudum (சுடும், 'burns, destroys'). If kolgai (கொள்கை, 'one's settled conduct', glossed by the commentators as ozhukkam) pizhaippin (பிழைப்பின், 'should fail'), it burns the kulam (குலம், 'family, lineage'). But naaninmai (நாணின்மை, 'shamelessness') nindra kadai (நின்றக் கடை, 'once it becomes settled') burns all nalam (நலம், 'every good'). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read the second fire as more total than the first; Kesikan says the first ruins only the family's standing while the second consumes everything. Kalaignar connects the lines: failing to feel shame at one's lapse lets ruin spread. Pope: ‘'Twill race consume if right observance fail; 'Twill every good consume if shamelessness prevail.’ The text (with the doubled consonant in நின்றக் கடை) is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நாண்அகத் தில்லார் இயக்கம் மரப்பாவை
நாணால் உயிர்மருட்டி அற்று.
transliteration:
Naanagath thillaar iyakkam marappaavai
naanaal uyirmarutti atru.
current_meaning: The movements of people with no shame in their hearts are like a wooden puppet jerked about on strings to fool onlookers into thinking it is alive.
elementary_explanation: Have you seen a puppet show? The puppet dances and waves, but it isn't really alive; someone is pulling strings. Valluvar says a person with no shame inside is like that: moving around, but with nothing real inside.
university_explanation: The chapter closes with a pun on naan (நாண்), which means both ‘shame’ and ‘cord, string’ (as in a bowstring). Those who lack naan agaththu (நாண் அகத்து, 'shame within') move like a marappaavai (மரப்பாவை, 'wooden doll, puppet') that, by naanaal (நாணால், 'by means of strings'), uyir maruttum (உயிர்மருட்டும், 'deceives people into thinking it has life'). Kesikan glosses the strings as the yantra cords of a mechanical doll, and Varadarasanar and Pappaiah describe a doll worked by rope to look alive. So the shameless are alive in appearance only, moved by outside pulls rather than by an inner moral life. The wordplay (shame in the first line, string in the second) is often singled out as one of Valluvar's finest. Pope: ‘'Tis as with strings a wooden puppet apes life's functions.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
கருமம் செயஒருவன் கைதூவேன் என்னும்
பெருமையின் பீடுடையது இல்.
transliteration:
Karumam seya oruvan kaithooven ennum
perumaiyin peedudaiyadhu il.
current_meaning: No greatness carries more dignity than a person's resolve, ‘I will not rest my hands from the work of raising my family.’
elementary_explanation: Imagine a girl who promises, ‘I will keep helping my family every day, and I won’t give up when it gets boring.’ Valluvar says that promise, kept day after day, is the proudest thing a person can wear, prouder than any medal.
university_explanation: The chapter opens by naming its ideal: the person who says kai thooven (கைதூவேன், ‘I will not let my hand rest’) in karumam (கருமம், ‘the work’), understood by Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan as the duty of raising one's kudi (குடி, ‘family, lineage, community’). Peedu (பீடு) means dignity or eminence, so the couplet ranks this self-imposed vow above every other form of perumai (பெருமை, ‘greatness’), the subject of chapter 98. Solomon Pappaiah widens kudi to ‘house and country’, a reading he keeps through the whole chapter, while Kesikan, in the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, keeps it to one's own family line. Pope renders it ‘Who says “I’ll do my work, nor slack my hand”, / His greatness, clothed with dignity supreme, shall stand.’ The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஆள்வினையும் ஆன்ற அறிவும் எனஇரண்டின்
நீள்வினையால் நீளும் குடி.
transliteration:
Aalvinaiyum aandra arivum ena irandin
neelvinaiyaal neelum kudi.
current_meaning: A family grows and lasts through sustained work that combines two things: manly effort and full knowledge.
elementary_explanation: Building a strong treehouse needs two things: strong arms to hammer and a smart plan so it doesn't fall. Valluvar says a family is the same: hard work plus good thinking, kept up for a long time, makes it grow tall.
university_explanation: The couplet names two instruments, aalvinai (ஆள்வினை, ‘manly exertion’, the theme of chapter 62) and aandra arivu (ஆன்ற அறிவு, ‘full, ripened knowledge’), and says that the neelvinai (நீள்வினை, ‘long, unbroken effort’) carried out with both makes the kudi neelum (நீளும், ‘lengthen, extend, flourish’). The play between neel- ‘long’ in the work and neel- ‘lengthen’ in the family is deliberate: duration in effort produces duration in the line. Pope captures this with ‘In deed prolonged, then lengthens out the race’s line.’ Kesikan and Varadarasanar both read the two as effort and knowledge joined in uninterrupted action; Karunanidhi adds ‘deep knowledge and perseverance.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
குடிசெய்வல் என்னும் ஒருவற்குத் தெய்வம்
மடிதற்றுத் தான்முந் துறும்.
transliteration:
Kudiseyval ennum oruvarkuth theyvam
madidhatruth thaanmun thurum.
current_meaning: When a person resolves ‘I will raise my family’, fortune itself tucks up its garment and hurries ahead to help.
elementary_explanation: Have you noticed that when you really decide to clean your room, things suddenly seem to fall into place? Valluvar says that when someone truly decides to lift up their family, it is as if heaven rolls up its sleeves and runs ahead to help.
university_explanation: The striking image is madi tharru (மடிதற்று, ‘having tucked up the fold of its garment’), the gesture of someone girding up to work or run, so that theyvam (தெய்வம்) mun urum (முந்துறும், ‘comes forward first’). Mu. Varadarasanar glosses theyvam as oozh (ஊழ், ‘destiny, fate’), keeping with the Kural's chapter 38; Solomon Pappaiah reads it as a deity tightening its garment; Karunanidhi, rationalising, calls it the force of nature known as divine action. Pope gives ‘With vest succinct the goddess leads the way.’ The verb kudiseyval (‘I will make my family’) is a first-person vow, continuing 1021. The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
சூழாமல் தானே முடிவெய்தும் தம்குடியைத்
தாழாது உஞற்று பவர்க்கு.
transliteration:
Soozhaamal thaane mudiveydhum thamkudiyaith
thaazhaadhu unjatru bavarkku.
current_meaning: For those who strive without delay to raise their family, the work reaches its goal by itself, even before they have planned it out.
elementary_explanation: When you practise piano every day without putting it off, one day a hard song just seems to play itself. Valluvar says that when people keep working for their family without delay, success often arrives before they even sit down to plan it.
university_explanation: Soozhaamal (சூழாமல், ‘without deliberating, without planning’) and thaane (தானே, ‘of itself’) frame the promise that the task mudiveydhum (முடிவெய்தும், ‘reaches completion’) for those who thaazhaadhu unjatrupavar (தாழாது உஞற்றுபவர், ‘strive without delay’). Kesikan, following the older commentary, attributes this to divine aid (தெய்வ உதவியால்), linking it to 1023; Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read it naturalistically, saying the capacity to finish comes to the prompt worker unsought. Karunanidhi has victories ‘pile up of themselves.’ Pope translates ‘Without a thought spontaneously, his end will gain.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
குற்றம் இலனாய்க் குடிசெய்து வாழ்வானைச்
சுற்றமாச் சுற்றும் உலகு.
transliteration:
Kutram ilanaaik kudiseydhu vaazhvaanaich
sutramaach chutrum ulagu.
current_meaning: The world gathers around the person who raises his family without doing wrong, and treats him as its own kin.
elementary_explanation: Think of a kind neighbour who works hard for her family and never cheats anyone. Soon the whole street treats her like family, bringing food and asking her advice. Valluvar says that is what happens to honest family-builders: everyone wants to be their relative.
university_explanation: Kutram ilanaai (குற்றம் இலனாய், ‘being without fault’) is the condition: the family must be raised by blameless means. The reward is a pun on sutram (சுற்றம், ‘kin, relatives’) and sutrum (சுற்றும், ‘surrounds, encircles’): the ulagu (உலகு, ‘world’) surrounds him as if it were his own relatives. Varadarasanar and Kesikan say people seek to become his kin; Pappaiah narrows ulagu to ‘the great’ (உயர்ந்தோர்), in keeping with the commentarial habit of reading ulagam as the worthy. Pope translates ‘The world shall circle him, and kindred claim.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
நல்லாண்மை என்பது ஒருவற்குத் தான்பிறந்த
இல்லாண்மை ஆக்கிக் கொளல்.
transliteration:
Nallaanmai enbadhu oruvarkuth thaanpirandha
illaanmai aakkik kolal.
current_meaning: True manliness means making oneself the one who leads and looks after the household one was born into.
elementary_explanation: Some people think being strong means winning fights. Valluvar says real strength is when you grow up and become the person your family can lean on, the one who takes care of things at home.
university_explanation: The couplet redefines nallaanmai (நல்லாண்மை, ‘good manliness, true valour’) by rhyming it with illaanmai (இல்லாண்மை, ‘mastery of the household’): real valour is aakkik kolal (ஆக்கிக் கொளல், ‘making one's own’) the governance of the home one was born in (thaan pirandha, தான் பிறந்த). Varadarasanar and Kesikan read it as taking on the ruling of one's birth-family; Pappaiah again extends it to house and country; Karunanidhi reverses the emphasis, saying the able ruler brings glory to the family of his birth. Pope gives ‘To him who gives his powers, the house from which he sprang to raise.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
அமரகத்து வன்கண்ணர் போலத் தமரகத்தும்
ஆற்றுவார் மேற்றே பொறை.
transliteration:
Amaragaththu vankannar polath thamaragaththum
aatruvaar metre porai.
current_meaning: Just as on the battlefield the burden falls on the fearless, so within a family the burden rests on those able to bear it.
elementary_explanation: In a soccer game, the toughest players stand in front when the other team attacks. Valluvar says families are the same: when trouble comes, the strongest, most capable person has to step forward and carry the load.
university_explanation: The couplet balances amaragaththu (அமரகத்து, ‘in the battlefield’) against thamaragaththum (தமரகத்தும், ‘among one's own people too’); the vankannar (வன்கண்ணர், ‘the hard-eyed, the fearless’) of war correspond to the aatruvaar (ஆற்றுவார், ‘those who are able’) in the family, and on them falls porai (பொறை, ‘burden, load’). Varadarasanar stresses that though many are born into a family, the burden lies on the capable. Text note: ytamizh.com reads தமரகத்தும் (with the inclusive -um) while thirukkural.net prints தமரகத்து ஆற்றுவார்; the meaning is the same and this edition follows the -um reading, which Pope's ‘Amid his kindred so’ also reflects.

tamil:
குடிசெய்வார்க் கில்லை பருவம் மடிசெய்து
மானங் கருதக் கெடும்.
transliteration:
Kudiseyvaark killai paruvam madiseydhu
maanang karudhak kedum.
current_meaning: Those who raise a family have no ‘right season’ to wait for; if they idle or stand on their dignity, the family is ruined.
elementary_explanation: If you wait for the ‘perfect day’ to do your chores, it never comes, and the mess just grows. Valluvar says people who care for a family can't wait for a perfect time or think a job is beneath them; they just have to get going.
university_explanation: Paruvam (பருவம், ‘season, proper time’) is denied to the kudiseyvaar (குடிசெய்வார், ‘those who make the family’): any time is the time. The second line names two enemies, madi (மடி, ‘sloth’, the theme of chapter 61) and maanam karudhal (மானம் கருதல், ‘considering one's pride or honour’), either of which makes the family kedum (கெடும், ‘perish’). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah read maanam as standing on one's dignity, refusing humble work; Karunanidhi reads it as being shaken by insults directed at oneself. Pope gives ‘Wait for no season, when you would your house uprear; / ’Twill perish, if you wait supine, or hold your honour dear.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம் கொல்லோ குடும்பத்தைக்
குற்ற மறைப்பான் உடம்பு.
transliteration:
Idumbaikke kolkalam kollo kudumbaththaik
kutra maraippaan udambu.
current_meaning: Is the body of one who shields his family from harm only a vessel for suffering?
elementary_explanation: Think of a parent who works late, carries heavy bags, and gets up at night when the baby cries. Their body is tired and sore. Valluvar asks: is that body only made for hardship? His answer is that their toil is also full of love and worth.
university_explanation: The couplet is a rhetorical question: is the udambu (உடம்பு, ‘body’) of the one who kutram maraippaan (குற்றம் மறைப்பான், ‘wards off harm’ from his kudumbam, குடும்பம், ‘family’) merely an idumbaikke kolkalam (இடும்பைக்கே கொள்கலம், ‘a vessel for suffering alone’)? The particle kollo (கொல்லோ) marks wonder or doubt. Varadarasanar reads it plainly as ‘is his body only a home for suffering?’, conceding the hardship; Kesikan and Pappaiah draw the implied answer, that it is also a vessel of joy; Karunanidhi says such a person is honoured as one born to bear suffering. Pope gives ‘Is not his body vase that various sorrows fill, / Who would his household screen from every ill?’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
இடுக்கண்கால் கொன்றிட வீழும் அடுத்தூன்றும்
நல்லாள் இலாத குடி.
transliteration:
Idukkankaal kondrida veezhum aduththoondrum
nallaal ilaadha kudi.
current_meaning: A family with no good person to stand by and prop it up will fall like a tree when misfortune strikes at its root.
elementary_explanation: A young tree needs a stick tied beside it so the wind doesn't knock it over. Valluvar says a family is like that tree: when hard times blow, it needs a strong, caring person standing beside it, or it will fall.
university_explanation: The image is of a tree: idukkan (இடுக்கண், ‘misfortune’) strikes at its kaal (கால், ‘foot, base’) and kondrida (கொன்றிட, ‘cutting, killing’) brings it down, unless there is a nallaal (நல்லாள், ‘good person’) who aduththu oondrum (அடுத்து ஊன்றும், ‘stands close and props it up’). Varadarasanar and Pappaiah make the axe explicit (துன்பமாகிய கோடாரி, ‘the axe of misfortune’), and Kesikan names the tree; Pappaiah reads nallaal as ‘good children’. The couplet closes the chapter by turning 1021's vow into a warning about its absence. Pope gives ‘When trouble the foundation saps the house must fall, / If no strong hand be nigh to prop the tottering wall.’ The text is identical on both sources.

tamil:
சுழன்றும்ஏர்ப் பின்னது உலகம் அதனால்
உழந்தும் உழவே தலை.
transliteration:
Suzhandrum-Erp pinnadhu ulagam adhanaal
uzhandhum uzhavae thalai.
current_meaning: However the world wanders from one trade to another, it still ends up following the plough; so, for all its hardship, farming is the foremost of occupations.
elementary_explanation: People can be bakers, builders, drivers or doctors, but every one of them still needs lunch, and lunch starts in a farmer's field. Farming is hard, sweaty work, yet Valluvar says it is the most important job of all, because every other job leans on it.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with its thesis: suzhandrum (சுழன்றும், 'though it whirls about', i.e. though people turn to many other callings) the world is Erp pinnadhu (ஏர்ப் பின்னது, 'behind the plough'), so uzhandhum (உழந்தும், 'even though it means toil') uzhavu is thalai (தலை, 'head, chief'). Puliyur Kesikan, in the commentarial line of Parimelazhagar, reads suzhandrum as people roaming through other trades because they see the hardship of farming, and the second line as a concession: farming is best despite that hardship; Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar agree. Uzhavu (ch. 104) stands in the Kudiyiyal section of Porutpal, between Kudiseyalvagai (ch. 103) and Nalkuravu (ch. 105, poverty), so Valluvar presents productive labour as the household's answer to want. The Tamil text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உழுவார் உலகத்தார்க்கு ஆணிஅஃ தாற்றாது
எழுவாரை எல்லாம் பொறுத்து.
transliteration:
Uzhuvaar ulagaththaarkku aaNi-aq thaatraadhu
ezhuvaarai ellaam poRuththu.
current_meaning: Those who plough are the linchpin of the world, because they carry everyone who cannot till the soil and turns to other work.
elementary_explanation: A wagon wheel has a small pin that holds it on the axle. Without that pin the wheel falls off and the whole cart stops. Valluvar says farmers are that pin: they feed everyone else, so the whole world keeps rolling because of them.
university_explanation: The image is the aaNi (ஆணி), the linchpin or axle-pin that keeps a cart's wheel in place; the ploughmen are the aaNi of ulagaththaar (உலகத்தார், 'the people of the world'). The second line gives the reason: aqthu aatraadhu ezhuvaarai ellaam poRuththu (அஃது ஆற்றாது எழுவாரை எல்லாம் பொறுத்து), 'bearing all who, unable to do that (ploughing), go off to other work'. Puliyur Kesikan, in the line of Parimelazhagar, glosses ezhuvaar as those who leave farming for other trades and are still fed by the farmers' grain; Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah read it the same way, and Pope gives 'linch-pin of the world'. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; ytamizh hyphenates the transliteration aaNi-aq.

tamil:
உழுதுண்டு வாழ்வாரே வாழ்வார்மற் றெல்லாம்
தொழுதுண்டு பின்செல் பவர்.
transliteration:
UzhudhuNdu vaazhvaarae vaazhvaarmaR Rellaam
thozhudhuNdu pinsel pavar.
current_meaning: Only those who live by ploughing and eating its yield truly live; everyone else eats by bowing to others and walks behind them.
elementary_explanation: Imagine growing your own tomatoes and eating them, compared with always having to ask someone else to share. Valluvar says the farmer who grows his own food can stand tall, while people who must keep asking others for food have to follow behind them.
university_explanation: The couplet sets uzhudhu uNdu (உழுது உண்டு, 'ploughing, eating') against thozhudhu uNdu (தொழுது உண்டு, 'bowing, eating'), a deliberate rhyme in which a single consonant separates self-reliance from servility. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, glosses those who plough as urimai vaazhvinar (உரிமை வாழ்வினர், 'those who live by right'), and says the rest eat by paying court to others and pinsel (பின்செல், 'follow behind') them; Solomon Pappaiah adds that the farmer ploughs for others as well as for himself. The ideal is economic independence rather than caste or rank. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
பலகுடை நீழலும் தங்குடைக்கீழ்க் காண்பர்
அலகுடை நீழ லவர்.
transliteration:
Palakudai neezhalum thangutaikkeezhk kaaNpar
alakutai neezha lavar.
current_meaning: Farmers whose wealth is the shade of ripening grain will see the shade of many kings' umbrellas gathered under their own king's umbrella.
elementary_explanation: In old Tamil kingdoms a king's royal umbrella stood for his rule. Valluvar says that a land with plenty of grain becomes so strong and attractive that other lands come under its protection. Good farms make a strong country.
university_explanation: The couplet plays on kudai (குடை, the royal parasol, emblem of sovereignty) and neezhal (நீழல், 'shade'). alakudai neezhalavar (அலகுடை நீழலவர்) are those who have the shade of alaku (அலகு, ears of grain), that is, prosperous farmers; Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, glosses them as nel udaiyavar, 'owners of paddy', and also as karunaiyaalar, 'the compassionate', taking neezhal as the cool shade of grace (thannali), a reading Mu. Varadarasanar keeps. Such farmers 'see' the umbrellas of many kings come under their own king's umbrella, because grain surplus makes a realm strong. Solomon Pappaiah takes a softer line: people of other lands come to desire the farmers' ruler. Pope's 'Whose fields are shaded by the waving grain' brings out the pun. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; only word spacing differs.

tamil:
இரவார் இரப்பார்க்கொன்று ஈவர் கரவாது
கைசெய்தூண் மாலை யவர்.
transliteration:
Iravaar irappaarkkondru eevar karavaadhu
kaiseydhooN maalai yavar.
current_meaning: Those whose way of life is to eat by the work of their own hands never beg, and they give to those who beg without hiding what they have.
elementary_explanation: A girl who grows her own strawberries never has to ask anyone for strawberries. And when a friend asks for some, she shares happily instead of hiding the basket. Working with your own hands lets you be both proud and generous.
university_explanation: kai seydhu ooN maalaiyavar (கைசெய்து ஊண் மாலையவர்) means 'those whose nature (maalai, மாலை) is to eat by the work of their hands'. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, identifies them with farmers (uzhavar) whose effort yields food. Two consequences follow: iravaar (இரவார், 'they do not beg') and they give irappaarkku ondru (இரப்பார்க்கு ஒன்று, 'something to those who beg') karavaadhu (கரவாது, 'without concealment'). Mu. Varadarasanar widens the subject to all who labour with their hands (thozhilaalar), while Solomon Pappaiah and Kesikan keep the focus on ploughing. The couplet also looks ahead to the later chapters Iravu (106) and Iravachcham (107) on begging. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
உழவினார் கைம்மடங்கின் இல்லை விழைவதூஉம்
விட்டேம்என் பார்க்கும் நிலை.
transliteration:
Uzhavinaar kaimmadangin illai vizhaivadhooum
vittaemen paarkkum nilai.
current_meaning: If the farmers fold their hands, even those who say 'we have given up everything we desired' cannot keep to their way of life.
elementary_explanation: Even people who have given up toys, money and fancy things to live a simple, holy life still need a bowl of rice each day. If farmers stopped working, those holy people would go hungry too. So everyone, even a saint, depends on the farmer.
university_explanation: uzhavinaar kai madangin (உழவினார் கை மடங்கின்) means 'if the ploughmen's hands fold (stop working)'. Then illai ... nilai (இல்லை ... நிலை): there is no standing even for those who say vizhaivadhooum vittaem (விழைவதூஉம் விட்டேம், 'we have renounced even what is desired'), that is, the ascetics (thuRavigaL). Puliyur Kesikan, in Parimelazhagar's line, takes vizhaivadhu as the food everyone desires and reads nilai as the renunciant's steadiness in his dharma; Solomon Pappaiah agrees, and Kalaignar says even renouncers must look to the farmer's hand. The couplet links back to the Aram section's chapter on ascetics (Neeththaar Perumai, ch. 3) and to rain as the support of austerity (Kural 19), placing the household economy beneath the renunciant. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net; the alapedai lengthening -ooum is printed in both.

tamil:
தொடிப்புழுதி கஃசா உணக்கின் பிடித்தெருவும்
வேண்டாது சாலப் படும்.
transliteration:
Thotippuzhudhi kaqsaa uNakkin pitiththeruvum
vaeNtaadhu saalap padum.
current_meaning: If ploughed soil is dried until one measure of it shrinks to a quarter, the crop will grow abundantly without even a handful of manure.
elementary_explanation: If you dig a garden, break up the lumps and let the sun dry the soil really well, the plants grow strong even without extra fertiliser. Getting the ground ready carefully is half the work of farming.
university_explanation: This is one of the Kural's most technical couplets. thodi (தொடி) and kaqsu (கஃசு) are weights: one palam and a quarter palam. thodippuzhudhi kaqsaa uNakkin (தொடிப்புழுதி கஃசா உணக்கின்) means 'if you dry a palam of ploughed dust down to a quarter-palam', that is, plough repeatedly and sun-dry the soil until three-quarters of its moisture weight is lost. Then piditheruvum vaeNdaadhu (பிடித்து எருவும் வேண்டாது, 'not needing even a fistful of manure') the crop saalap padum (சாலப் படும், 'will flourish greatly'). Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar give this measure-based reading, following Parimelazhagar; Solomon Pappaiah converts it to about 35 grams reduced to 8.75 grams, and Kalaignar stresses repeated ploughing. Pope keeps the weights as 'ounce' and 'quarter-ounce'. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
ஏரினும் நன்றால் எருவிடுதல் கட்டபின்
நீரினும் நன்றதன் காப்பு.
transliteration:
Erinum nandraal eruvidudhal kattapin
neerinum nandradhan kaappu.
current_meaning: Manuring is better than ploughing, and once the weeds are cleared, guarding the crop is better even than watering it.
elementary_explanation: Planting a garden is not the end of the job. You feed the soil, pull out the weeds, and then you have to protect the plants from birds, goats and trampling feet. Watching over what you grew matters even more than watering it.
university_explanation: The couplet ranks the farmer's tasks: eruviduthal (எருவிடுதல், 'applying manure') is better than Er (ஏர், 'ploughing'), and after katta (கட்ட, 'weeding'; Kesikan and Varadarasanar gloss kattapin as 'after removing weeds') kaappu (காப்பு, 'guarding, protection') is better than neer (நீர், 'watering'). Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, reads the sequence as plough, manure, weed, water, guard, with each later step more decisive than the one before it; Kalaignar's paraphrase ranks weeding and watering as 'very good' and protection as best. The point is that the work ends with vigilant protection of what has been produced, a principle the Porutpal applies to wealth as well as crops. tamil:
செல்லான் கிழவன் இருப்பின் நிலம்புலந்து
இல்லாளின் ஊடி விடும்.
transliteration:
Sellaan kizhavan iruppin nilampulandhu
illaaLin ooti vidum.
current_meaning: If the owner stays at home and does not go out to his land, the land will sulk and turn away from him like a neglected wife.
elementary_explanation: If you plant a garden and then forget about it, the plants droop and the weeds take over, as if the garden were upset with you. Valluvar says land is like a family member: it needs you to show up and care for it every day.
university_explanation: kizhavan (கிழவன்) here means 'owner' (of the land), not 'old man'; sellaan iruppin (செல்லான் இருப்பின்) means 'if he stays without going (to the field)'. The land then pulandhu (புலந்து, 'feeling aggrieved') and oodi vidum (ஊடி விடும், 'turns away in sulking') like an illaaL (இல்லாள், 'wife'). The verbs pulavi and oodal are technical terms of the Kamaththuppal for a lover's quarrel (compare chapters 131-133), so Valluvar borrows the vocabulary of love to describe neglected land. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, glosses that the owner must go daily and do what is needed; Solomon Pappaiah spells out that the land, like a wife, first withers inwardly and then withholds its yield. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இலமென்று அசைஇ இருப்பாரைக் காணின்
நிலமென்னும் நல்லாள் நகும்.
transliteration:
Ilamendru asaii iruppaaraik kaaNin
nilamennum nallaaL nakum.
current_meaning: When the good lady called Earth sees people sitting idle and saying 'we have nothing', she laughs to herself.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone sitting beside a big empty field and complaining, 'I have nothing to eat!' Valluvar says the Earth would giggle, because the field is right there, ready to grow food for anyone willing to work it.
university_explanation: ilam endru (இலம் என்று, 'saying "we have nothing"') and asaii iruppaar (அசைஇ இருப்பார், 'those who sit idle', with asaii lengthened by alapedai) are the people the Earth laughs at. nilam ennum nallaaL (நிலம் என்னும் நல்லாள்) means 'the good woman called Earth', and nakum (நகும்) means 'will laugh'. Puliyur Kesikan, following Parimelazhagar, says she laughs to herself, because the remedy for their poverty lies in her and needs only effort; Solomon Pappaiah reads the laughter as mockery, and Kalaignar names her Bhoomiththaai (Mother Earth). The chapter ends where it began, with land as the answer to want, and leads directly into Nalkuravu (ch. 105, Poverty). Pope's rendering is 'The earth, that kindly dame, will laugh to see, / Men seated idle pleading poverty.' The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்மையின் இன்னாதது யாதெனின் இன்மையின்
இன்மையே இன்னா தது.
transliteration:
Inmaiyin innaadhadhu yaadhenin inmaiyin
inmaiyae innaa thadhu.
current_meaning: If you ask what is more painful than poverty, the only answer is poverty itself; it has no equal among sorrows.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone asking, “What hurts more than a really bad toothache?” and the answer is, “Only a really bad toothache.” Valluvar says being so poor that you have nothing is like that: there is nothing else to compare it with, because it is the worst hurt of its kind.
university_explanation: The chapter opens with a deliberately circular definition built on repetition of inmai (இன்மை, ‘not-having, want’): inmaiyin innaadhadhu (‘what is more grievous than want’) is answered by inmaiyae (‘want itself’). Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar both gloss inmaiyin as a comparative (‘like poverty’), so the sense is that poverty is its own only standard of comparison; Kalaignar makes the same point by saying no other sorrow can serve as an upamai (simile) for it. The figure is a classic Tamil ananvaya-like device in which the subject is compared to itself to mark it as incomparable, and Pope’s ‘Nothing pains more than poverty, save poverty alone’ preserves the tautology. Nalkuravu (நல்குரவு) in the chapter title is the standard classical word for destitution; placed in the Kudiyiyal right after Uzhavu (ch. 104, agriculture, the remedy for want) and before Iravu (ch. 106, begging), the chapter traces the social consequences of losing one’s means. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net apart from spacing.

tamil:
இன்மை எனவொரு பாவி மறுமையும்
இம்மையும் இன்றி வரும்.
transliteration:
Inmai enavoru paavi maRumaiyum
immaiyum indri varum.
current_meaning: The wicked one called poverty, once it comes, robs a person of both the joys of this life and the good of the next.
elementary_explanation: Think of a villain in a story who sneaks in and takes away both your lunch today and your treat for tomorrow. Valluvar calls poverty a villain like that: it takes away the good things you could enjoy now, and also the good you could do for others, which helps you later.
university_explanation: Valluvar personifies inmai as oru paavi (ஒரு பாவி), ‘a sinner, a wicked one’, a vivid figure for an abstract condition. The second line says it comes so that maRumai (மறுமை, the next world) and immai (இம்மை, this world) are both lost. Solomon Pappaiah spells out the logic the commentators share: the poor cannot give to others, so they lose the merit that secures the next world, and they have nothing to enjoy themselves, so they lose this world too; Puliyur Kesikan likewise speaks of losing worldly pleasure here and the bliss of heaven hereafter. Sivayogi Sivakumar instead reads the pair temporally (present and future), and Kalaignar secularises it as loss of peace now and later. The Kural thus ties wealth to aram (virtue) through the duty of giving, a link developed in the Arathuppaal chapters on Eekai (giving) and Oppuravu (helpfulness). The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
தொல்வரவும் தோலும் கெடுக்கும் தொகையாக
நல்குரவு என்னும் நசை.
transliteration:
Tholvaravum thoalum kedukkum thogaiyaaga
nalkuravu ennum nasai.
current_meaning: The hungry craving called poverty destroys, all at once, a family’s ancient standing and its good name.
elementary_explanation: Imagine a family that has been known for generations as kind and honest. If someone in it becomes so desperate that wanting things takes over, they might do things that spoil the family’s good name all at once, like one spill ruining a whole painting.
university_explanation: The key word is nasai (நசை, ‘desire, craving’): Valluvar does not just say nalkuravu but ‘nalkuravu ennum nasai’, the craving that is called poverty, suggesting that destitution shows itself as a gnawing want. Tholvaravu (தொல்வரவு) is ‘what has come down from of old’, the dignity or heritage of one’s line, and thoal (தோல்) is read by Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Puliyur Kesikan as pugazh (fame, honour); the English explanation carried on ytamizh.com renders it ‘the dignity of one’s speech’, reflecting an older reading that associates thoal with elevated, well-formed words. Thogaiyaaga (‘all together, at a stroke’) stresses the suddenness of the ruin. Kalaignar shifts the causation slightly, saying that poverty breeds greed which then ruins lineage and fame. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இற்பிறந்தார் கண்ணேயும் இன்மை இளிவந்த
சொற்பிறக்கும் சோர்வு தரும்.
transliteration:
IRpiRandhaar kaNNaeyum inmai iLivandha
soRpiRakkum soarvu tharum.
current_meaning: Poverty breeds, even in people of good family, a weariness from which mean and shameful words come out.
elementary_explanation: When you are very tired and hungry, you might snap at someone even though you are usually polite. Valluvar says being very poor can make even well-brought-up people so worn down that unkind or embarrassing words slip out.
university_explanation: IRpiRandhaar (இற்பிறந்தார்) are ‘those born in a (good) house’, i.e. of noble family, and the -um of kaNNaeyum (‘even in them’) concedes that breeding is no protection. Inmai gives soarvu (சோர்வு, ‘slackness, exhaustion, lapse of vigilance’) from which iLivandha sol (இளிவந்த சொல், ‘words that bring disgrace’) is born. Mu. Varadarasanar, Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar all read it this way: poverty causes the lapse, and the lapse produces demeaning speech. Puliyur Kesikan, notably, reverses the causation, saying that the slackness which leads to base acts is itself what brings poverty even to good families, a reading that turns the couplet into a warning rather than a lament. Pope’s ‘Oblivion that gives birth to words that bring disgrace’ takes soarvu as forgetfulness of one’s station. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நல்குரவு என்னும் இடும்பையுள் பல்குரைத்
துன்பங்கள் சென்று படும்.
transliteration:
Nalkuravu ennum idumbaiyuL palkuraith
thunbangaL sendru padum.
current_meaning: Within the single affliction called poverty, sorrows of every kind gather and take root.
elementary_explanation: Have you seen one leak in a roof let in rain that ruins the carpet, the books and the bed? Valluvar says poverty is like that one leak: many other troubles come pouring in through it.
university_explanation: Idumbai (இடும்பை, ‘affliction, distress’) names poverty as one trouble, and palkurai (பல்குரை, ‘of many kinds’) thunbangaL (‘sorrows’) are said to ‘go and settle’ (sendru padum) within it. Puliyur Kesikan and Solomon Pappaiah read this as all sorrows being contained in poverty, so that poverty is the sum of misfortunes; Mu. Varadarasanar says they ‘arise and grow’ inside it; Kalaignar reverses the image slightly, with many sorrows springing out of poverty. Either way poverty is the matrix of other ills, which prepares for the later couplets on lost respect (1046), estranged kin (1047) and sleepless dread (1048-1049). Pope’s ‘Attendant sorrows plenteous grow’ follows the ‘springing up’ reading. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நற்பொருள் நன்குணர்ந்து சொல்லினும் நல்கூர்ந்தார்
சொற்பொருள் சோர்வு படும்.
transliteration:
NaRporuL nangunarndhu sollinum nalkoorndhaar
soRporuL soarvu padum.
current_meaning: Even when the poor speak sound truths they have fully understood, their words are disregarded and come to nothing.
elementary_explanation: Imagine two children giving the same right answer in class, but everyone only listens to the one with the fancy new shoes. Valluvar noticed that people often ignore what poor people say, even when it is wise, and that this is unfair.
university_explanation: NaRporuL (நற்பொருள்) is ‘good matter’, which Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar specify as the sense of good books (nool), and nangunarndhu (‘having understood well’) stresses that the speaker is genuinely learned. Yet the soRporuL (சொற்பொருள், ‘the meaning of the words’) of nalkoorndhaar (நல்கூர்ந்தார், ‘those who have become poor’) suffers soarvu, here ‘failure, lapse’: it is not heard or heeded. The same word soarvu that meant inner weariness in 1044 here describes the social fate of the poor man’s speech, a deliberate echo. Solomon Pappaiah puts it simply: if the speaker is poor, his words are not honoured. Pope’s ‘Their sense from memory of mankind will fade away’ takes the lapse as being forgotten. The observation is descriptive and critical, not an endorsement of the bias. The text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
அறஞ்சாரா நல்குரவு ஈன்றதா யானும்
பிறன்போல நோக்கப் படும்.
transliteration:
ARanjaaraa nalkuravu eendradhaa yaanum
piRanpoala noakkap padum.
current_meaning: One sunk in poverty that has no connection with virtue is looked upon as a stranger even by the mother who bore him.
elementary_explanation: A mother’s love is the strongest love there is. Valluvar warns that if someone becomes poor because of bad choices and also turns away from doing right, people may turn away from him, and even his own family may feel hurt and distant.
university_explanation: The decisive qualifier is aRanjaaraa (அறஞ்சாரா, ‘not joined to aram, virtue’). Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan read it as ‘poverty not in keeping with virtue’, i.e. destitution that is unrighteous in cause or accompaniment; Solomon Pappaiah glosses it as poverty without just reasons; Kalaignar makes it moral, the person who abandons virtue because of poverty. Eendra thaai (ஈன்ற தாய், ‘the mother who bore him’) is the strongest possible bond, and piRan poala (‘like another, a stranger’) marks its collapse. Read with the qualifier, the couplet does not say that every poor person is rejected, only that want combined with the loss of aram estranges even the closest kin. The ytamizh.com English explanation (‘reduced to absolute poverty’) passes over aRanjaaraa, a reminder that translations differ on how much moral weight to give it. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
இன்றும் வருவது கொல்லோ நெருநலும்
கொன்றது போலும் நிரப்பு.
transliteration:
Indrum varuvadhu kolloa nerunalum
kondradhu poalum nirappu.
current_meaning: The poor man asks in dread: will the want that all but killed me yesterday come upon me again today?
elementary_explanation: Imagine having a very scary day, and waking up the next morning worried: “Will it happen again today?” Valluvar says a very poor person feels like that every single day, afraid that yesterday’s hunger and worry will come back.
university_explanation: The couplet is spoken in the voice of the poor man himself, an unusual dramatic touch in the Porutpaal. Nirappu (நிரப்பு, ‘want, need’) is a synonym of nalkuravu, and the particle kolloa (கொல்லோ) marks anxious questioning: ‘will it come today too?’. Nerunal (நெருநல், ‘yesterday’) and kondradhu poalum (‘as though it killed’) describe the daily ordeal as a near-death; Puliyur Kesikan adds the implied cry ‘if it comes, what shall I do?’, while Mu. Varadarasanar frames it as the poor man’s daily trembling. Kalaignar reads it as a longing that it may not return. The present-tense dread contrasts with the general statements of the earlier couplets and leads into the sleeplessness of 1049. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
நெருப்பினுள் துஞ்சலும் ஆகும் நிரப்பினுள்
யாதொன்றும் கண்பாடு அரிது.
transliteration:
NeruppinuL thunjalum aagum nirappinuL
yaadhondrum kaNpaadu aridhu.
current_meaning: A man may somehow sleep in the midst of fire, but in the midst of want he can by no means close his eyes.
elementary_explanation: Have you ever been so worried that you could not fall asleep? Valluvar says that worrying about having no food or money is so strong that it is even harder to sleep than if you were lying next to a fire.
university_explanation: The hyperbole sets two ‘insides’ side by side: neruppinuL (‘within fire’) and nirappinuL (‘within want’). Thunjal (துஞ்சல், ‘sleeping’) is said to be possible (aagum) in the first, while kaNpaadu (கண்பாடு, ‘the closing of the eyes, sleep’) is aridhu (‘rare, hard’) in the second, yaadhondrum (‘by any means at all’). Puliyur Kesikan explains how sleeping in fire might be possible, through the help of mantra and medicine, and Solomon Pappaiah through yogic power; Pappaiah also narrows nirappu to the torment of hunger. Mu. Varadarasanar and Kalaignar keep the image general. The couplet follows naturally from 1048: the dread of tomorrow’s want is what keeps the poor awake. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

tamil:
துப்புர வில்லார் துவரத் துறவாமை
உப்பிற்கும் காடிக்கும் கூற்று.
transliteration:
Thuppura villaar thuvarath thuRavaamai
uppiRkum kaadikkum koottru.
current_meaning: When the utterly destitute do not renounce the world completely, they only become death to other people’s salt and gruel.
elementary_explanation: Imagine someone who has nothing and keeps taking a little salt and soup from the neighbours, but does nothing else with his life. Valluvar says that person should either change his life completely or choose a simple life of giving things up, instead of just using up what others need.
university_explanation: Thuppuravu (துப்புரவு) means the things one enjoys or lives by, so thuppuravillaar are ‘those without any means’. Thuvara (‘completely’) thuRavaamai (‘not renouncing’) is the fault named: Puliyur Kesikan and Mu. Varadarasanar say the only course left to such people is full renunciation, and failing it they are merely koottru (கூற்று, Yama, death) to uppu (salt) and kaadi (காடி, sour rice-water or gruel; Pope’s ‘vinegar’). Solomon Pappaiah sharpens the social point: by staying in household life they consume the salt and gruel in other people’s homes. Kalaignar reads thuppuravu as orderliness, so the subject becomes those impoverished by disorderly living. The chapter thus ends by pointing toward thuRavu (renunciation), linking the Porutpaal back to the Thuravaraviyal of the first book, and leads into Iravu (begging) in ch. 106. The Tamil text matches on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.
